stimulus: Computer programmers usually remark that computing ma chines, with a perfect want of discrimination, will do any silly thing they are asked to do. The reason for this lies, for sure, in the narrow fixation of the computing machine’s “intelligence” on the details of its ow n perceptions—its inability to be instructed by any large context. In a psychological portrayal of the com puter intelligence, three connected adjectives come to mind: single-minded, literal-minded, and simpleminded. Recognizing this, we should at the same moment recognize that this single-mindedness, literal-mindedn ess, and simplemindedness also features theoretical mathematics, though to a lesser extent. Since science seeks to deal with reality, even the most accurate scien ces normally work with more or less imperfectly comprehended approximations toward which scientists must maintain an appropriate skepticism. Therefore, for example, it may come as a shock to math ematicians to learn that the Schrodinger equation for the hydrogen atom is not a literally correct portrayal of this atom, but merely an approximation to a somewhat more correct equation taking account of spin, magnetic dipol e, and relativistic effects; and that such corrected equation is itself merely an imperfect approximation to an infinite set of quantum field-theoretical equations. Physicists, looking at the initial Schrodinger equation, learn to sense in it the presence of many invisible terms in addition to the differential terms visible, and this se nse inspires a completely appropriate disregard for the purely technical characteristics of the equation. This ve ry healthy skepticism is foreign to the mathematical approach. Mathematics must deal with well-defined situations. Therefore, mathematicians depend on an intellectual effort outside of mathematics for th e essential specification of the approximation that mathematics is to take literally. Provide mathematicians a situation that is the least bit ill-defined, and they will make it well-defined, perhaps appropriately, but perhaps inappropriately. In some cases, the mathematicians’ literal-mindedness may have unfortunate results. The mathematicians turn th e scientists’ theoretical assumptions, that is, their convenient points of analytical emphasis, into axioms, and then take th ese axioms literally. This brings the danger that they may also persuade the scientists to take these axioms literally. The question, central to the scientific investigation but immensely disturbing in the mathematical context—what happens if the axioms are relaxed?—is thus ignored. The physicist correctly dreads accurate argument, because an argument that is cogent only if it is accurate loses all its force if the assumptions on which it is based are slightly altered, whereas an argument that is cogent though inaccurate may well be stable under small perturbations of its underlying assumptions.
prompt: The author discusses computing ma chines in the first paragraph primarily in order to do which of the following?

options.text: Indicate the dangers inherent in relying to a great extent on machines
Illustrate his views about the approach of mathematicians to problem solving
Compare the work of mathematicians with that of computer programmers
Provide one definition of intelligence
Emphasize the importance of computers in modern technological society

are unable to accept mathematical explanations of natural phenomena

stimulus: The determination of the sources of copper ore utilized in the manufacture of copper and bronze artifacts of Bronze Age civilizations would add greatly to our know ledge of cultural contacts and trade in that era. Researchers have plumbed artifacts and ores for their concentrations of elements, but for a variety of reasons, these studies have typically failed to furnish evidence of the sources of the copper utilized in the objects. Elemental composition can diversify within the same c opper-ore lode, often due to varying admixtures of other elements, particularly iron, lead, zinc, and arsenic . And high concentrations of cobalt or zinc, noticed in several artifacts, appear in a variety of copper-ore sources. Furthermore, the processing of ores introduced poorly regulated changes in the concentrations of mi nor and trace elements in the resulting metal. Some elements evaporate during smelting and roasting; disparate temperatures and processes generate disparate degrees of loss. Eventually, flux, which is sometimes added during smelting to remove waste material from the ore, could add quantities of elements to the ultimate product. A rudimentary property that is unchanged through these chemical processes is the isotopic composition of every metallic element in the ore. Isotopic compos ition, the percentages of the diverse isotopes of an element in a given sample of the element, is thereby especially suitable as an indicator of the sources of the ore. Of course, for this purpose it is requisite to di scover an element whose isotopic composition is more or less steady throughout a given ore body, but diversifies from one copper ore body to another or, at least, from one geographic region to another. The ideal choice, when isotopic composition is employ ed to investigate the source of copper ore, would seem to be copper itself. It has been shown that dimi nutive but measurable variations occur naturally in the isotopic composition of copper. Howeve r, the variations are significant enough merely in rare ores; between samples of the common ore minerals of copper, isotopic variations greater than the measurement error have not been discovered. An alternative option is lead, wh ich occurs in most copper and bronze artifacts of the Bronze Age in amounts consistent with the lead bein g derived from the copper ores and probably from the fluxes. The isotopic composition of lead often varies fro m one source of common copper ore to another, with variations exceeding the measurement error; and preliminary studies imply virtually uniform isotopic composition of the lead from a single copper-ore source. While some of the lead discovered in an artifact may have been introduced from flux or when other metals were added to the copper ore, lead so added in Bronze Age processing would often have the same isotopic compos ition as the lead in the copper ore. Lead isotope studies may in turn prove beneficial for interpreting the archaeological record of the Bronze Age.
prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: discuss the techniques of analyzing lead isotope composition
propose a way to determine the origin of the copper in certain artifacts
resolve a dispute concerning the analysis of copper ore
describe the deficiencies of a currently used method of chemical analysis of certain metals
offer an interpretation of the archaeological record of the Bronze Age

explanation: 正確答案為 B（propose a way to determine the origin of the copper in certain artifacts）。文章先說明元素組成分析無法找出銅礦來源，再提出同位素組成、並以鉛同位素作為可行指標。D 缺陷只是鋪陳，並非主旨；A 文章並未討論鉛同位素的實際分析技術。

stimulus: Classical physics defines the vacuum as a state of void: a vacuum is said to exist in a region of space if there is nothing in it. In the quantum field theories that delin eate the physics of elementa ry particles, the vacuum becomes somewhat more complex. Even in empty space, particles can appear spontaneously by virtue of fluctuations of the vacuum. For instance, an electron and a positron, or antielectron, can be innovated out of the absence. Particles innovated in this way have only a transient existence; they are annihilated almost as soon as they occur, and their presence can never be detect ed directly. They are called virtual particles in order to discriminate them from real particles, whose lifetimes are not restrained in the same way, and which can be detected. Therefore it is still possible to define that vacuum as a space that has no real particles in it. One might expect that the vacuum would always be the state of lowest probable energy for a given region of space. If an area is originally empty and a real partic le is put into it, the whole energy, it seems, should be raised by at least the energy equivalent of the mass of the added particle. A surprising consequence of some recent theoretical investigations is that such assumption is not invariably real. There are conditions under which the introduction of a real particle of finite mass into an empty region of space can reduce the whole energy. If the reduction in energy is enormous enough , an electron and a positron will be spontaneously innovated. Under these conditions the electron and positron are not a conseque nce of vacuum fluctuations but are real particles, which exist indefinitely and can be detected. In other words, under these conditions the vacuum is an unsteady state and can decay into a state of lower energy; i.e., one in which real particles are innovated. The crucial condition for the decay of the vacuum is the presence of an intense electric field. Resulting from the decay of the vacuum, the space pervaded by such a field can be said to acquire an electric charge, and it can be called a charged vacuum. The particles that ma terialize in the space make the charge manifest. An electric field of sufficient intensity to create a charged v acuum is prone to be found in solely one place: in the immediate vicinity of a superheavy atomic nucleus, one with about twice as many protons as the heaviest natural nuclei known. A nucleus that large cannot be steady, but it might be probable to assemble one next to a vacuum for long enough to observe the decay of the vacuum. Experiments attempting to accomplish this are now under way.

stimulus: Of the thousands of specimens of meteorites found on Earth and known to science, only about 100 are igneous; that is, they have undergone melting by volcanic acti on at some time since the planets were first created. Achondrites are the only known samples of volcanic rocks originating outside the Earth-Moon sy stem. Most are thought to have been dislodged by interbody impact from asteroids, with diameters of from 10 to 500 kilometers, in solar orbit between Mars and Jupiter. The great opposition to the Ma rtian origin of shergottites is the absence of lunar meteorites on Earth. An impact capable of ejecting a fragment of the Martian surface into an Earth-intersecting orbit is even less possible than such an event on the Moon, in view of the Moon’s smaller size and closer proximity to Earth. A recent study indicates, however, that permafrost ices below the surface of Mars may have changed the effects of impact on it. If the ices had been quickly vaporized by an impacting object, the increasing gases might have helped the ejected fragments reach escape velocity. Eventually, analyses performed by space probes show a uncommon ch emical similarity between Martian soil and the shergottites.

stimulus: It has been known for many decades that the appearance of sunspots is approximately periodic, with an average cycle of eleven years. Moreover, the incidence of solar flares and the flux of solar cosmic rays, ultraviolet radiation, and x-radiation a ll vary directly with the sunspot cycle. But after more than a century of exploration the relation of these and other phenomena, know n jointly as the solar-activity cycle, to terrestrial weather and climate remains confused. For instant, th e sunspot cycle and the allied magnetic-polarity cycle have been associated with periodicities detected in r ecords of such variables as rainfall, temperature, and winds. Invariably, however, the relation is weak, and commonly of dubious statistical significance. Effects of solar variability over longer terms have also been sought. The nona ppearance of recorded sunspot activity in the notes kept by European observers in the late seventeenth and early eighteenth centuries has made scholars assume a concise cessation of sunspot activity at that time (a period called the Maunder minimum). The Maunder minimum has been linked to a span of uncommon cold in Europe extending from the sixteenth to the early nineteen th centuries. The reality of the Maunder minimum has yet to be accepted, however, especially since the records that Chinese naked-eye observers of solar activity made at that time appear to challenge it. Scientists have also sought evidence of long-term solar periodicities by examining oblique climatological data, such as fossil records of the thickness of ancient tree rings. These studies, however, failed to link unambiguously terrestrial climate and the solar-activity cycle, or even to confirm the cycle’s past existence. If constant and trustworthy geological or archaeologi cal evidence tracing the solar-activity cycle in the distant past could be found, it might also address an si gnificant issue in solar physics: how to model solar activity. Currently, there are two models of solar activit y. The first supposes that the Sun’s internal motions (caused by rotation and convection) interface with its large-scale magnetic field to create a dynamo, a device in which mechanical energy is cha nged into the energy of a magnetic field. stimulus: One of the easiest and best known kinds of crystal is the ionic salt, of which a representative example is sodium chloride or ordinary table salt. The essential constituents of an ionic salt are ions: atoms or molecules that have become electrically charged by obtaining or losing one or more electrons. In forming sodium chloride, for instance, sodium atoms give up an electron (thereby becoming positively charged) and chlorine atoms gain an electron (thereby becoming negatively ch arged). The ions are drew to one another by their opposite charges, and they stack together tightly, like compactly packed spheres. Recently, scientists at Michigan State University developed a new kind of crystal called an electride. In electrides, the anions (negative ions ) are entirely replaced by electrons, which are trapped in innately formed cavities within a framework of constantly stacked cations (positive ions). Electrides are the first examples of ionic salts in which all these anionic sites are occupied merely by electrons. Unlike other types of anions, anioni c electrons do not behave as if they were easy charged spheres. In particular, because of their low mass and their trend to interface with one another over great distances, they cannot be “pinned down” to any one location. Instead , they wander close to and among the atoms lining the cavity and interface with electrons in nearby cavities, perhaps altering places with them. The properties of an electride rely greatly on the distance between the cavities that hold trapped electrons. When the trapped electrons are far apart, they do not interface powerfully, and so behave somewhat like an array of isolated negative charges. When they are closer together, they begin to display properties related with large ensembles of unanimous particles. When they ar e still closer, the ensemble properties control and the electrons “delocalize”: they are no longer compactly bound within individual cavities but are more or less free to pass through the spaces within the frame-work of positive ions. By composing electrides from a diversity of material s, one can vary the geometry of the anionic cavities and their relation to the surrounding cations. The resu lting properties may make it possible for electrides to become a basis for economically practical new material s and devices. For example, because the electrons in some electrides are very weakly bound, these crystals c ould be effective as photosensitive detectors, in which an impinging photon liberates an electron, leading to a tiny electric current. The same weak binding could also make electrides practical in solar-energy converters and as cathodes in batteries. One encumbrance is the trend of electrides to break down through reaction with air and water. Scientists are seeking ways to promote their steadiness.

stimulus: Many objects in daily use have distinctly been affect ed by science, but their form and function, their dimensions and appearance, were controlled by t echnologists, artisans, designers, inventors, and engineers—using non-scientific modes of thought. Many features and qualities of the objects that a technologist thinks about cannot be reduced to unequivocal verbal depictions; they are dealt with in the mind by a visual, nonverbal process. In the development of Western technology, it has been non-verbal thinking, by and large, that has fixed the outlines and filled in the details of our material surroundings. Pyramids, cathedrals, and rockets exist not because of geometry or thermodynamics, but because they were first an image in the minds of those who create them. The innovative shaping process of a technologist’s mind can be seen in almost every artifact that exists. For instance, in designing a diesel engine, a technologist might impress individual ways of nonverbal thinking on the machine by constantly using an inherent sense of rightness and fitness. What would be the shape of the combustion chamber? Where should the valves be placed? Should it have a long or short piston? Such questions have a range of answers that are supplied by e xperience, by physical requirements, by restrictions of available space, and not least by a sense of form. Some decisions, such as wall thickness and pin diameter, may rely on scientific calculations, but the nonscientific component of design remains principal. Design courses, then, should be an crucial element in engineering curricula. Nonverbal thinking, a central mechanism in engineering design, includes perceptions, the stock-in-trade of the artist, not the scientist. Because perceptive processes are not supposed to entail “hard thinking,” nonverbal thought is sometimes seen as a original stage in the development of cognitive processe s and inferior to verbal or mathematical thought. But it is contradictory that when the staff of the Historic American Engineering Record wished to have drawings made of machines and isometric views of indus trial processes for its historical record of American engineering, the only college students with the requis ite abilities were not engineering students, but rather students attending architectural schools. If courses in design, which in a powerfully analyt ical engineering curriculum offer the background required for realistic problem-solving, are not provided, we can expect to encounter foolish but expensively mistakes occurring in leading-edge engineering system s. For instance, early models of high-speed railroad cars loaded with complicated controls were unable to operate in a snowstorm because a fan sucked snow into the electrical system. ridiculous arbitrary failures that plague automatic control systems are not only trivial aberrations; they are a reflection of the chaos that resu lts when design is assumed to be principally a problem in mathematics.
prompt: In the passage, the author is primarily concerned with

options.text: identifying the kinds of thinking that are used by technologists
stressing the importance of nonverbal thinking in engineering design
proposing a new role for nonscientific thinking in the development of technology
contrasting the goals of engineers with those of technologists
criticizing engineering schools for emphasizing science in engineering curricula

explanation: 正確答案為 B（stressing the importance of nonverbal thinking in engineering design）。作者主張技術成品的形式多由非語言思考決定，以柴油引擎為例，並主張設計課程應是工程課程的重要部分，否則會出現昂貴錯誤，重點在強調非語言思考對工程設計的重要。E 太偏，作者是建議增加設計課程，並非批評學校重視科學。

stimulus: As of the late 1980’s, neither theorists nor large-scale computer climate models could exactly forecast whether cloud systems would help or hurt a warming globe. So me investigations indicated that a four percent augmentation in stratocumulus clouds over the ocean could compensate for a doubling in atmospheric carbon dioxide, preventing a possibly disastrous planetwide temp erature increase. On the other hand, an increase in cirrus clouds could enhance global warming. That clouds stood for the weakest element in climate models was demonstrated by a study of fourteen such models. Contrasting climate forecasts for a wo rld with double the current amount of carbon dioxide, scientists found that the models agreed quite well if clouds were not involved. options.text: confirming a theory
supporting a statement
presenting new information
predicting future discoveries
reconciling discrepant findings

stimulus: The origin of the theory that principal geologic events may occur at regular intervals can be traced back not to an investigation of volcanism or plate tectonics but to a study of marine extinctions. In the early 1980’s, researchers began to look carefully at the question of how these extinctions occur. Two paleontologists, Raup and Sepkoski, compiled a master list of marine species that died out during the past 268 million years and observed that there were brief periods during which many species disappeared at once. These extensive extinctions occurred at astonishingly regular intervals. Later studies divulged that extinctions of terrestri al reptiles and mammals also occurred periodically. These findings, integrated with the research of Raup and Sepkoski, made scientists assume the presence of some kind of cyclically reoccurring force powerful enoug h to influence living things greatly. Speculation that so strong a force might influence geologic events as well made geologists search for evidence of periodicity in episodes of volcanism, seafloor spreading, and plate movement.

studying plate tectonics and the occurrence of volcanism over the past 268 million years
examining extinctions of marine species over the past 268 million years
finding out whether a rhythmically recurring geologic force exists
confirming previous evidence suggesting that extinction of terrestrial species occurred regularly

explanation: 正確答案為 C（examining extinctions of marine species over the past 268 million years）。文中說兩人「compiled a master list of marine species that died out during the past 268 million years」，研究的是海洋物種滅絕。D 錯在週期性力量是後來科學家根據其發現所作的推測，並非他們研究的目的；B 則是地質學家後來才做的研究。

stimulus: Benjamin Franklin established that lightning is the tran sfer of positive or negative electrical charge between regions of a cloud or from cloud to earth. Such transfers demand that electrically neutral clouds, with uniform charge distributions, become electrified by separation of charges into disparate regions. The greater this separation is, the greater the voltage, or electrical potential of the cloud. Scientis ts still do not know the accurate distribution of charges in thunderclouds nor how separation suff icient to support the huge voltages typical of lightning bolts arises. In terms of one hypothesis, the precipitation theory, charge separation occurs resulting from precipitation. Larger droplets in a thunde rcloud precipitate downward past smaller suspended droplets. Collisions amid droplets transfer negative ch arge to precipitating droplets, leaving the suspended droplets with a positive charge, therefore generating a positive dipole in which the lower region of the thundercloud is full of negatively charged raindrops and the upper with positively charged suspended droplets.
prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with discussing which of the following?

options.text: A central issue in the explanation of how lightning occurs
Benjamin Franklin’s activities as a scientist
Research into the strength and distribution of thunderstorms
The direction of movement of electrical charges in thunderclouds
The relation between a cloud’s charge distribution and its voltage

explanation: 正確答案為 A（A central issue in the explanation of how lightning occurs）。文章指出科學家 still do not know…how separation sufficient to support the huge voltages…arises，並介紹 precipitation theory 作為一種解釋，即討論閃電成因中的核心問題（電荷分離）。B 富蘭克林只是開頭；E 只是背景說明。

As each source is activated, it produces a wave train that moves downward at a speed dete rmined solely by the rock’s elastic characteristics. As rock interfaces are crossed, the el astic features encountered typically change abruptly, which engenders part of the energy to be reflected back to the surface, where it is recorded by seismic instruments. The seismic records must be processed to redress for positional discr epancies between the source and the receiver, for unrelated wave trains, and for multiple reflections from th e rock interfaces. Then the data acquired at each of the specific source locations are amalgamated to genera te a physical profile of the subsurface, which can eventually be harnessed to select targets for drilling.
prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with

options.text: describing an important technique
discussing a new method
investigating a controversial procedure
announcing a significant discovery
promoting a novel application

explanation: 正確答案為 A（describing an important technique）。首句稱 seismic-reflection 是尋找石油 most salient tool，其後依序說明震源排列、波傳遞與反射、記錄處理與資料整合，是在描述一項重要技術。選項 discussing a new method 不對，文中說它 remains the most salient tool，並無「新」的意思。

stimulus: Scholars usually fail to see that music played a signifi cant role in the preservation of African culture in the United States. They precisely note that slavery stri pped some cultural elements from Black people—their political and economic systems—but they underrate the importance of music in sustaining other African cultural values. African music, unlike the music of some other cultures, was based on a whole vision of life in which music was not an isolated social domain. In African culture music was predominant, serving not only religion, but all phases of life, including birth, death, work, and play. The measures that a community devises to perpetuate itself come into being to maintain aspects of the cultural legacy that that community perceives as essential. Music, like art generally, was so inextricably a part of African culture that it became a critical means of preserving the culture during and after the dislocations of slavery.
prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: analyze the impact that slavery had on African political and economic systems
review the attempt of recent scholarship to study the influence of African music on other music
correct the failure of some scholars to appreciate the significance of music in African culture
survey the ways by which people attempt to preserve their culture against the effects of oppression
compare the relative importance of music with that of other art forms in culture

explanation: 正確答案為 C（correct the failure of some scholars to appreciate the significance of music in African culture）。首句指出學者「usually fail to see」音樂在保存美國非裔文化中的重要角色，後文說明非洲音樂貫穿生活各層面，因而成為保存文化的關鍵，目的在糾正學者的忽視。A 政治經濟制度的喪失只是學者正確注意到的背景。

stimulus: Conventionally, pollination by wind has been viewed as a reproductive process marked by random events in which the vagaries of the wind are compensated for by th e generation of vast quantities of pollen, so that the ultimate production of new seeds is guaranteed at the co st of generating much more pollen than is actually utilized. Since the potential hazards pollen grains are subj ect to as they are transported over long distances are immense, wind-pollinated plants have, in the view a bove, compensated for the ensuing loss of pollen through happenstance as a result of generating an amount of pollen that is one to three orders of magnitude greater than the amount produced by species pollinated by insects. However, a number of characteristics that are typical of wind-pollinated plants reduce pollen waste. For instance, numerous wind-pollinated species fail to rel ease pollen when wind speeds are low or when humid conditions predominates. Recent studies proffer another way in which speci es compensate for the inefficiency of wind pollination. These researches s uggest that species frequently take advantage of the physics of pollen motion by producing specific aerodynamic environments within the immediate vici nity of their female reproductive organs. It is the morphology of these organs that dictates the pattern of airflow disturbances through which pollen must travel. The speed and direc tion of the airflow disturbances can blend with the physical properties of a species’ pollen to generate a species-specific pattern of pollen collision on the surfaces of female reproductive organs. Provided that these surfaces are strategically located, the results of this combination can intensely increase the pollen-capture efficiency of a female reproductive organ. A crucial question that remains to be replied is whether the morphological attributes of the female reproductive organs of wind-pollinated species are evolu tionary adaptations to wind pollination or are only fortuitous. A complete resolution of the question is as yet impossible since adaptation must be estimated for each species within its own unique functional context. Ho wever, it must be said that, while evidence of such evolutionary adaptations does exist in some species, one must be meticulous about attributing morphology to adaptation. For instance, the spiral arrangement of scale-bract complexes on ovule-bearing pine cones, where the female reproductive organs of conifers are located, is significant to the production of airflow patterns that spiral over the cone’s surfaces, therefore passing airborne pollen from one scale to the next. However, these patterns cannot be viewed as an adaptation to wind pollination since the spiral arrangement appears in a number of non-wind-pollinated plant lineages and is considered as a characteristic of vascular plants, of which conifers are merely one kind, as a whole. Thus, the spiral arrangement is not likely to be the consequence of a direct adaptation to wind pollination.
prompt: The author of the passage is primarily concerned with discussing

options.text: the current debate on whether the morphological attributes of wind-pollinated plants are evolutionary adaptations
the kinds of airflow patterns that permit wind-pollinated plants to capture pollen most efficiently
the ways in which the reproductive processes of wind-pollinated plants are controlled by random events
a recently proposed explanation of a way in which wind-pollinated plants reduce pollen waste
a specific morphological attribute that permits one species of wind-pollinated plant to capture pollen

explanation: 正確答案為 D（a recently proposed explanation of a way in which wind-pollinated plants reduce pollen waste）。文章在介紹傳統觀點後，重點放在「Recent studies proffer another way」：雌性生殖器官的形態造成特定氣流，提高捕捉花粉的效率，之後再討論這是否為演化適應。A 的爭論只是延伸問題；E 太窄，文中並非談單一物種。

stimulus: Conventionally, pollination by wind has been viewed as a reproductive process marked by random events in which the vagaries of the wind are compensated for by th e generation of vast quantities of pollen, so that the ultimate production of new seeds is guaranteed at the co st of generating much more pollen than is actually utilized. Since the potential hazards pollen grains are subj ect to as they are transported over long distances are immense, wind-pollinated plants have, in the view a bove, compensated for the ensuing loss of pollen through happenstance as a result of generating an amount of pollen that is one to three orders of magnitude greater than the amount produced by species pollinated by insects. For instance, numerous wind-pollinated species fail to rel ease pollen when wind speeds are low or when humid conditions predominates. Recent studies proffer another way in which speci es compensate for the inefficiency of wind pollination. These researches s uggest that species frequently take advantage of the physics of pollen motion by producing specific aerodynamic environments within the immediate vici nity of their female reproductive organs. It is the morphology of these organs that dictates the pattern of airflow disturbances through which pollen must travel. The speed and direc tion of the airflow disturbances can blend with the physical properties of a species’ pollen to generate a species-specific pattern of pollen collision on the surfaces of female reproductive organs. Provided that these surfaces are strategically located, the results of this combination can intensely increase the pollen-capture efficiency of a female reproductive organ. A crucial question that remains to be replied is whether the morphological attributes of the female reproductive organs of wind-pollinated species are evolu tionary adaptations to wind pollination or are only fortuitous. A complete resolution of the question is as yet impossible since adaptation must be estimated for each species within its own unique functional context. Ho wever, it must be said that, while evidence of such evolutionary adaptations does exist in some species, one must be meticulous about attributing morphology to adaptation. For instance, the spiral arrangement of scale-bract complexes on ovule-bearing pine cones, where the female reproductive organs of conifers are located, is significant to the production of airflow patterns that spiral over the cone’s surfaces, therefore passing airborne pollen from one scale to the next. stimulus: Over the years, biologists have suggested two major pathways by which sexual selection may have shaped the evolution of male birdsong. In the first, male competition and intrasexual selecti on generate comparatively short, simple songs employed mainly in territorial behavior. In the second, female choice and intersexual selection generate longer, more comp lex songs employed mainly in ma te attraction; like this visual ornamentation as the peacock’s tail, elaborate vocal features enhance the male’s chances of being selected as a mate, and he thus enjoys more reproductive success than his less ostentatious rivals. The two pathways are not mutually exclusive, and we can exp ect to discover examples that reflect their interaction. Teasing them apart has been a significant challenge to evolutionary biologists. Early studies confirmed the role of intrasexual selection. In a variety of experiments in the field, males responded aggressively to recorded songs by displayi ng territorial behavior close to the speakers. The breakthrough for research into intersexual selection came in the amelioration of a new technique for investigating female response in the laboratory. When female cowbirds ra ised in isolation in sound-proof chambers were exposed to recordings of male song, they responded by displaying mating behavior. By quantifying the responses, researchers we re able to decide what particular characteristics of the song were most significant. In further experiments on song sparro ws, researchers discovered that when exposed to a single song type repeated several times or to a repertoire of diverse song types, females responded more to the latter. The beauty of the experimental design is that it efficiently rules out confounding variables; acoustic isolation guarantees that the female can respond merely to the song structure itself. If intersexual selection operates as hypothesized, males w ith more complex songs should not only attract females more readily but should also enjoy larger re productive success. At first, however, researchers doing fieldwork with song sparrows discovered no connection between greater repertoires and early mating, which has been shown to be one indicator of reproductive success; further, common measures of male quality utilized to foresee reproductive success, such as weight, size, age, and terr itory, also failed to correlate with song complexity. The confirmation researchers had been seeking was ev entually accomplished in research involving two varieties of warblers. Unlike the song sparrow, which repeats one of its several song types in bouts before switching to another, the warbler constantly com poses much longer and more variable songs without repetition. For the first time, research ers discovered a important correlation between repertoire size and early mating, and they found further that repertoire size had a more important effect than any other measure of male quality on the number of young produced. The evidence s uggests that warblers use their utterly elaborate songs primarily to attract females, clearly documenting the effect of intersexual selection on the evolution of birdsong.

stimulus: Picture-taking is a technique both for annexing th e unbiased world and for conveying the singular self. Photographs describe impartial realities that already ex ist, though only the camera can disclose them. And they describe an individual photographer’s temperament, finding itself through the camera’s cropping of reality. That is, photography has two opposite ideals: in the first, photography is about the world and the photographer is a just scrutinize who counts for little; but in the second, photography is the instrument of fearless, questing and the photographer is all. These conflicting ideals arise from a essential uneasiness on the part of both photographers and viewers of photographs toward the hostile constituent in “taking” a picture. Accordingly, the ideal of a photographer as observer is appealing because it implicitly denies that picture-taking is an hostile act. The issue, of course, is not so clear-cut. What photographers do cannot be ch aracterized as simply pred atory or as simply, and virtually, benevolent. As a consequence, one ideal of pi cture-taking or the other is always being rediscovered and advocated. An significant result of the coex istence of these two ideals is a recurrent ambivalence toward photography’s means. Whatever the claims that photography might make to be a form of individual expression on a par with painting, its ingenuity is inextricably rela ted to the powers of a machine. The steady growth of these powers has made possible the remarkable informativeness and creative formal beauty of many photographs, like Harold Edgerton’s high-speed photographs of a bullet hitting its target or of the swirls and eddies of a tennis stroke. But as cameras become more complicated, more automated, some photographers are tempted to disarm themselves or to indicate that they ar e not really armed, preferring to submit themselves to the limits forced by premodern camera technology becau se a cruder, less high-powered machine is thought to give more absorbing or emotional results, to leave more room for innovative accident. For instance, it has been essentially a point of honor fo r many photographers, including Walker Evans and Cartier-Bresson, to reject to use modern equipment. These photographers ha ve come to suspect the value of the camera as an instrument of “fast seeing.” Cartier-Bresson, in fact, claims that the modern camera may see too fast. This ambivalence toward photographic means determines tendencies in taste. The cult of the future (of faster and faster seeing) alternates over time with the wish to return to a purer past—when pictures had a handmade quality. This nostalgia for some immaculate state of the photographic enterprise is at present wide-ranging and underlies the present-day ardor for daguerreotypes and the wok of forgotten nineteenth-century provincial photographers. Photographers and viewers of photographs, it seems, need periodically to withstand their own knowingness.

stimulus: The making of classifications by literary historians can be a somewhat hazardous enterprise. When Black poets are discussed respectively as a group, for example, the extent to which their work reflects the development of poetry in general should not be forgotten, or a distortion of literary history may result. This caution is especially related in an assessment of the distin ctions between Black poets at the turn of the century (1900-1909) and those of the generation of the 1920’s . These distinctions incorporate the bolder and more straightforward speech of the later generation and its technical ingeniousness. It should be remembered, though, that comparable distinctions also existed for similar generations of White poets. When poets of the 1910’s and 1920’s are considered together, however, the differences that literary historians might make between “conservative” and “experimental” would be of little importantce in a discussion of Black poets, although these remain useful classifications for White poets of these decades. Certainly distinctions can be noted between “conservative” Black poets such as Counter Cullen and Claude McKay and “experimental” ones such as Jean Toomer and Langston Hughes. But Black poets were not battling over old or new styles; rather, one accomplished Black poet was ready to greet another, whatever his or her style, for what mattered was ethnic pride. However, in the 1920’s Black poets did dispute whether they should deal with especially ethnic subjects. They asked whether they should merely write about Bl ack experience for a Black audience or whether such demands were restrained. It may be said, though, that essentially all these poets wrote their excellent poems when they spoke out of racial feeling, race being, as James Weldon Johnson rightly put it, “perforce the thing the Negro poet knows best.” At the turn of the century, by contrast, most Black poets usually wrote in the conventional manner of the age and expressed noble, if vague, emotions in their poe try. These poets were not generlly gifted, though Roscoe Jamison and G. M. McClellen may be referred as exceptions. They chose not to write in dialect, which, as Sterling Brown has indicated, “meant a rejection of ster eotypes of Negro life,” and they refused to write only about ethnicsubjects. This rejection had both a ener getic and a passive consequence. As Brown observes, “Valuably insisting that Negro poets should not be li mited to issues of race, these poets committed [an] error… they refused to look into their hearts an d write.” These are significant insights, but one must emphasize that this rejection to look within was also representative of most White poets of the United States at the time. They, too, often turned from their own experience and fainlly created not very unforgettable poems about indefinite topics, such as the peace of nature.

When Black poets are discussed respectively as a group, for example, the extent to which their work reflects the development of poetry in general should not be forgotten, or a distortion of literary history may result. This caution is especially related in an assessment of the distin ctions between Black poets at the turn of the century (1900-1909) and those of the generation of the 1920’s . These distinctions incorporate the bolder and more straightforward speech of the later generation and its technical ingeniousness. It should be remembered, though, that comparable distinctions also existed for similar generations of White poets. When poets of the 1910’s and 1920’s are considered together, however, the differences that literary historians might make between “conservative” and “experimental” would be of little importantce in a discussion of Black poets, although these remain useful classifications for White poets of these decades. Certainly distinctions can be noted between “conservative” Black poets such as Counter Cullen and Claude McKay and “experimental” ones such as Jean Toomer and Langston Hughes. But Black poets were not battling over old or new styles; rather, one accomplished Black poet was ready to greet another, whatever his or her style, for what mattered was ethnic pride. However, in the 1920’s Black poets did dispute whether they should deal with especially ethnic subjects. They asked whether they should merely write about Bl ack experience for a Black audience or whether such demands were restrained. It may be said, though, that essentially all these poets wrote their excellent poems when they spoke out of racial feeling, race being, as James Weldon Johnson rightly put it, “perforce the thing the Negro poet knows best.” At the turn of the century, by contrast, most Black poets usually wrote in the conventional manner of the age and expressed noble, if vague, emotions in their poe try. These poets were not generlly gifted, though Roscoe Jamison and G. M. McClellen may be referred as exceptions. They chose not to write in dialect, which, as Sterling Brown has indicated, “meant a rejection of ster eotypes of Negro life,” and they refused to write only about ethnicsubjects. This rejection had both a ener getic and a passive consequence. As Brown observes, “Valuably insisting that Negro poets should not be li mited to issues of race, these poets committed [an] error… they refused to look into their hearts an d write.” These are significant insights, but one must emphasize that this rejection to look within was also representative of most White poets of the United States at the time. They, too, often turned from their own experience and fainlly created not very unforgettable poems about indefinite topics, such as the peace of nature.
prompt: According to the passage, an issue facing Black poets in the 1920’s was whether they should

options.text: seek a consensus on new techniques of poetry
write exclusively about and for Blacks
withdraw their support from a repressive society
turn away from social questions to recollect the tranquility of nature
identify themselves with an international movement of Black writers

explanation: 正確答案為 B（write exclusively about and for Blacks）。1920 年代詩人爭論 "whether they should merely write about Black experience for a Black audience"，merely 正對應 exclusively。尋求新技巧共識是陷阱，作者明言他們 "were not battling over old or new styles"。

stimulus: “Masterpieces are dumb,” wrote Flaubert, “They have a peaceful aspect like the very products of nature, like large animals and mountains.” He might have been thinking of War and Peace, that vast, quiet work, unpredictable and simple, stimulating eternal questions th rough the majesty of its being. Tolstoi’s simplicity is “overpowering,” says the critic Bayley, “disconcerting,” because it comes from “his arbitrary assumption that the world is as he sees it.” Like other nineteenth-century Russian writers he is “impressive” because he “means what he says,” but he stands apart from all othe rs and from most Western writers in his identity with life, which is so complete as to make us disremember he is an artist. He is the center of his work, but his egocentricity is of aunusual kind. Goethe, for instance , says Bayley, “cared for nothing but himself. Tolstoi was nothing but himself.” For all his diverse modes of writing and the abundance of characters in his fiction, Tolstoi and his work are of a piece. The well-known “conversion” of his middle years, emotionally recounted in his Confession, was a culmination of his early metaphysical life, not a departure from it. The obviously essential changes that led from epic narrative to dogmatic parable, from a jo yful, cheerful attitude toward life to pessimism and cynicism, from War and Peace to The Kreutzer Sonata, came from the same restless, susceptible depths of an self-sufficient spirit yearning to get at the truth of its experience. “Truth is my hero,” wrote Tolstoi in his youth, reporting the fighting in Seba ol. Truth remained his he ro—his own, not others’, truth. Others were awed by Napoleon, believed that a single man could alter the d estinies of nations, adhered to unintelligible rituals, formed their tastes on established canons of art. Tolstoi reversed all preconceptions; and in every reversal he overthrew the “system,” the “machine,” the outwardly or dained belief, the traditional behavior in favor of unmethodical, impetuous life, of inward motivation and the solutions of independent thought. In his work the feigned and the genuine are always exhibited in remarkable antagonism: the supposedly great Napoleon and the truly great, unregarded little Captain Tushin, or Nicholas Rostov’s real experience in battle and his later account of it. The simple is alwa ys pitted against the complicated, knowledge gained from observation against assertions of borrowed faiths. Tolstoi’s miraculous simplicity is a product of these tensions; his work is a record of the questions he put to him self and of the answers he found in his search. The greatest characters of his fiction epitomize this search, and thei r joyfulness relies on the measure of their answers. Tolstoi wanted joyfulness, but only hard-won joyfuln ess, that emotive fulfillment and intellective clarity which could come merely as the prize of all-consuming effort. He despised lesser satisfactions.
prompt: Which of the following best characterizes the author’s attitude toward Tolstoi?

options.text: She deprecates the cynicism of his later works.
She finds his theatricality artificial.
She admires his wholehearted sincerity.
She thinks his inconsistency disturbing.
She respects his devotion to orthodoxy.

explanation: 正確答案為 C（She admires his wholehearted sincerity.）。作者稱讚 Tolstoi「means what he says」、與生活認同到讓人忘了他是藝術家，並以「Truth is my hero」強調他忠於自身真實，整體是欣賞其全心全意的真誠。A 錯：作者只是陳述後期轉向 pessimism，並未加以貶抑。

stimulus: “I want to condemn the social system, and to show it at work, at its most intense.” Virginia Woolf’s infuriating statement about her intentions in writing Mrs. Dalloway has commonly been ignored by the critics, since it stresses an aspect of her literary interests very distin ct from the conventional picture of the “poetic” novelist concerned with examining states of reverie and vision and with following the complex pathways of personal consciousness. But Virginia Woolf was a realistic as well as a poetic novelist, a satirist and social critic as well as a visionary: literary critics’ cavalier dismissal of Woolf’s social vision will not withstand scrutiny. In her novels, Woolf is greatly engaged by the que stions of how individuals are formed(or deformed) by their social environments, how historical forces impinge on people’s lives, how class, wealth, and gender help to determine people’s fates. Most of her novels are based on a realistically rendered social setting and in a accurate historical time. Woolf’s focus on society has not been commonly acknowledged because of her strong hostility to propaganda in art. The pictures of reformers in her nove ls are frequently satiric or greatly critical. Even when Woolf is essentially compassionate to their cau ses, she describes people anxious to improve their society and possessed of a message or program as arroga nt or devious, unaware of how their political ideas serve their own psychological needs. (Her Writer’ s Diary notes: “the only candid people are the artists,” whereas “these social reformers and philanthropists…harbor…discreditable desires under the disguise of loving their kind…”) Woolf detested what she called “preaching” in fiction, too, and condemned novelist D. H. Lawrence (among others) for working by this method. Woolf’s own social criticism is conveyed in the language of observation rather than in straightforward commentary, since for her, fiction is a pensive, not an active art. She depicts phenomena and offers materials for a judgment about society and social issues; it is the reader’s work to put the observations together and comprehend the constant point of opinion behind them. As a moralist, Woolf works by indirection, subtly undermining officially accepted mores, mocking, indica ting, calling into question, rather than asserting, supporting, bearing witness: hers is the satirist’s art. Woolf’s literary models were incisive social observers like Chekhov and Chaucer. As she put it in The Common Reader, “It is safe to say that not a single law has been framed or one stone set upon another because of anything Chaucer said or wrote; and yet, as we read him, we are assimilating morality at every pore.” Like Chaucer, Woolf chose to comprehend as well as to judge, to know her society root and branch—a decision significant in order to develop art rather than polemic.

stimulus: Extraordinary innovative activity has be en featured as revolutionary, flying in the face of what is established and generating not what is acceptable but what will become accepted. With respect to this formulation, highly innovative activity transcends the limits of an existing form and establishes a new principle of organization. However, the idea that extraordinary creativity transcends established limits is misleading when it is applied to the arts, although it may be cogent for the sciences. Di screpancies between highly innovative art and highly innovative science arise in part from a difference in their goals. For the sciences, a novel theory is the goal and end result of the innovative act. Creative science gene rates new propositions in terms of which disparate phenomena can be connected to one another in more coherent ways. Such phenomena as a brilliant diamond or a nesting bird are relegated to the role of data, serving as the means for formulating or testing a novel theory. The goal of highly creative art is very disparate: the phenomenon itself becomes the direct product of the creative act. Shakespeare’s Hamlet is not a tract about the behavior of indecisive princes or the uses of political power; nor is Picasso’s painting Guernica primarily a propositional statement about the Spanish Civil War or the evils of fascism. What highly creative artistic activity generates is not a new generalization that transcends established limits, but rather an aesthetic pa rticular. Aesthetic particulars endangered by the highly innovative artist extend or exploit, in a creative way, the limits of an existing form, rather than transcend that form. This is not to deny that a highly innovative artist sometimes establishes a new principle of organization in the history of an artistic field; the composer Montev erdi, who created music of the highest aesthetic worth, comes to mind. More typically, however, whether or not a composition establishes a new principle in the history of music has little bearing on its aesthetic value. Since they embody a new principle of organization, some musical works, such as the operas of the Florentin e Camerata, are of signal historical significance, but few listeners or musicologists would contain these am ong the great works of music. On the other hand, Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro is certainly among the masterpieces of music even though its modest creations are confined to extending existing means. It has been said of Beethoven that he toppled the rules and freed music from the stifling confines of convention. Bu t a close study of his compositions unveils that Beethoven overturned no foundational rules. Rather, he was an incomparable strategist who exploited limits—the forms, rules, and conventions that he inherited from predecessors such as Mozart and Haydn, Bach and Handel—in strikingly original ways.

stimulus: Extraordinary innovative activity has be en featured as revolutionary, flying in the face of what is established and generating not what is acceptable but what will become accepted. With respect to this formulation, highly innovative activity transcends the limits of an existing form and establishes a new principle of organization. However, the idea that extraordinary creativity transcends established limits is misleading when it is applied to the arts, although it may be cogent for the sciences. Di screpancies between highly innovative art and highly innovative science arise in part from a difference in their goals. For the sciences, a novel theory is the goal and end result of the innovative act. Creative science gene rates new propositions in terms of which disparate phenomena can be connected to one another in more coherent ways. Such phenomena as a brilliant diamond or a nesting bird are relegated to the role of data, serving as the means for formulating or testing a novel theory. The goal of highly creative art is very disparate: the phenomenon itself becomes the direct product of the creative act. Shakespeare’s Hamlet is not a tract about the behavior of indecisive princes or the uses of political power; nor is Picasso’s painting Guernica primarily a propositional statement about the Spanish Civil War or the evils of fascism. What highly creative artistic activity generates is not a new generalization that transcends established limits, but rather an aesthetic pa rticular. Aesthetic particulars endangered by the highly innovative artist extend or exploit, in a creative way, the limits of an existing form, rather than transcend that form. This is not to deny that a highly innovative artist sometimes establishes a new principle of organization in the history of an artistic field; the composer Montev erdi, who created music of the highest aesthetic worth, comes to mind. More typically, however, whether or not a composition establishes a new principle in the history of music has little bearing on its aesthetic value. Since they embody a new principle of organization, some musical works, such as the operas of the Florentin e Camerata, are of signal historical significance, but few listeners or musicologists would contain these am ong the great works of music. On the other hand, Mozart’s The Marriage of Figaro is certainly among the masterpieces of music even though its modest creations are confined to extending existing means. It has been said of Beethoven that he toppled the rules and freed music from the stifling confines of convention. Bu t a close study of his compositions unveils that Beethoven overturned no foundational rules. Rather, he was an incomparable strategist who exploited limits—the forms, rules, and conventions that he inherited from predecessors such as Mozart and Haydn, Bach and Handel—in strikingly original ways.

options.text: is cited with high frequency in the publications of other scientists
is accepted immediately by the scientific community
does not relegate particulars to the role of data
presents the discovery of a new scientific fact
introduces a new valid generalization

explanation: 正確答案為 E（introduces a new valid generalization）。文中說創新科學「generates new propositions」以連貫解釋各種現象，藝術產生的則「not a new generalization」，由對比可知科學創新在於提出新通則。C 反了，科學正是把具體事物「relegated to the role of data」；D 新事實並非文中所說的目標。

stimulus: Initially the Vinaver hypothesis that Malory’s eight romances, once thought to be fundamentally unified, were in effect eight independent works generated both a sense of relief and an unpleasing shock. Vinaver’s hypothesis comfortably explained away the apparent c ontradictions of chronology and made each romance independently satisfying. It was, however, disagreeable to discover that what had been thought of as one book was now eight books. Part of this response was the common reaction to the disturbance of set ideas. Nevertheless, even nowadays, after lengthy consid eration of the hypothesis’ refined but legitimate observations, one cannot avoid the conclusion that the ei ght romances are merely one work. options.text: discuss the validity of a hypothesis

propose guidelines for future argument
stipulate conditions for acceptance of an interpretation
deny accusations about an apparent contradiction

stimulus: “Popular art” has a number of meanings, impossible to determine with any precision, which range from folklore to junk. The poles are clear enough, but the middle tends to blur. The Hollywood Western of the 1930’s, for instance, has elements of folklore, but is closer to junk than to high art or folk art. There can be great trash, just as there is bad high art. The musicals of George Gershwin are great popular art, never aspiring to high art. Schubert and Brahms, however, used elements of popular music—folk themes—in works distinctly intended as high art. The case of Verdi is a distinct one: he took a welcomed genre—bourgeois melodrama set to music (an accurate definition of ni neteenth-century opera)—and, without changing its essential nature, transformed it into high art. This rema ins one of the greatest accomplishments in music, and one that cannot be completely admired without acknowledging the crucial trashiness of the genre. As an example of such a transmutation, think ab out what Verdi made of the representative political elements of nineteenth-century opera. Generally in th e plots of these operas, a hero or heroine—frequently depicted just as an personal, unrestrained by class —is caught between the unethical corruption of the aristocracy and the doctrinaire inflexibility or secret greed of the leaders of the proletariat. Verdi transforms this naive and unlikely formulation with music of exceptional energy and rhythmic vitality, music more slight than it seems at first hearing. There are scenes and arias that still sound like calls to arms and were distinctly comprehended as such when they were first perform ed. Such pieces lend an immediacy to the otherwise veiled political message of these operas and call up feelings beyond those of the opera itself. Or consider Verdi’s treatment of character. Before Verdi, there were scarcely any characters at all in musical drama, only a series of situations which made the singers convey a series of emotive states. Any attempt to find consistent psychological portrayal in these operas is misplaced creativity. The only consistency was the singer’s vocal technique: when the cast altered, new arias were nearly always substituted, usually adapted from other operas. Verdi’s characters, on the other hand, have genuine conformity and rectitude, even if, in many cases, the conformity is that of pasteboard melodrama. The rectitude of the character is achieved through the music: once he had become established, Ve rdi did not recreate his music for different singers or countenance alterations or substitu tions of somebody else’s arias in one of his operas, as every eighteenth-century composer had done. When he revised an opera, it was just fo r impressive economy and effectiveness.

that their works are examples of great trash

a contrast between the conventions of nineteenth-century opera and those of other musical forms
that popular music could be employed in compositions intended as high art

explanation: 正確答案為 E（that popular music could be employed in compositions intended as high art）。作者在列舉流行藝術各種情形時說，Schubert 與 Brahms 在「works distinctly intended as high art」中使用了民謠主題，說明流行音樂元素可用於高雅藝術作品。A 的與 Verdi 比較高下、C 的影響關係，文中都沒有提到。

The Hollywood Western of the 1930’s, for instance, has elements of folklore, but is closer to junk than to high art or folk art. There can be great trash, just as there is bad high art. The musicals of George Gershwin are great popular art, never aspiring to high art. Schubert and Brahms, however, used elements of popular music—folk themes—in works distinctly intended as high art. The case of Verdi is a distinct one: he took a welcomed genre—bourgeois melodrama set to music (an accurate definition of ni neteenth-century opera)—and, without changing its essential nature, transformed it into high art. This rema ins one of the greatest accomplishments in music, and one that cannot be completely admired without acknowledging the crucial trashiness of the genre. As an example of such a transmutation, think ab out what Verdi made of the representative political elements of nineteenth-century opera. Generally in th e plots of these operas, a hero or heroine—frequently depicted just as an personal, unrestrained by class —is caught between the unethical corruption of the aristocracy and the doctrinaire inflexibility or secret greed of the leaders of the proletariat. Verdi transforms this naive and unlikely formulation with music of exceptional energy and rhythmic vitality, music more slight than it seems at first hearing. There are scenes and arias that still sound like calls to arms and were distinctly comprehended as such when they were first perform ed. Such pieces lend an immediacy to the otherwise veiled political message of these operas and call up feelings beyond those of the opera itself. Or consider Verdi’s treatment of character. Before Verdi, there were scarcely any characters at all in musical drama, only a series of situations which made the singers convey a series of emotive states. Any attempt to find consistent psychological portrayal in these operas is misplaced creativity. The only consistency was the singer’s vocal technique: when the cast altered, new arias were nearly always substituted, usually adapted from other operas. Verdi’s characters, on the other hand, have genuine conformity and rectitude, even if, in many cases, the conformity is that of pasteboard melodrama. The rectitude of the character is achieved through the music: once he had become established, Ve rdi did not recreate his music for different singers or countenance alterations or substitu tions of somebody else’s arias in one of his operas, as every eighteenth-century composer had done. When he revised an opera, it was just fo r impressive economy and effectiveness.
prompt: According to the passage, the immediacy of th e political message in Verdi’s operas stems from the

options.text: vitality and subtlety of the music
audience’s familiarity with earlier operas
portrayal of heightened emotional states
individual talents of the singers
verisimilitude of the characters

explanation: 正確答案為 A（vitality and subtlety of the music）。文中說 Verdi 用「music of exceptional energy and rhythmic vitality」轉化這種政治情節，音樂比初聽時更細膩，這些段落「lend an immediacy」給原本隱晦的政治訊息。C 的情緒狀態描述的是 Verdi 之前的歌劇。

stimulus: Practically speaking, the artistic maturing of the cinema was the single-handed accomplishment of David W. Griffith (1875-1948). Before Griffith, photography in im pressive films composed of little more than placing the actors before a static camera and showing them in full length as they would have appeared on stage. From the beginning of his career as a director, however, Griff ith, because of his love of Victorian painting, used composition. He conceived of the camera image as having a prospect and a rear ground, as well as the middle distance preferred by most directors. By 1910 he was em ploying close-ups to disclose important details of the scene or of the acting and exceeding long shots to obtai n a sense of spectacle and distance. His appreciation of the camera’s possibilities created novel impressive effects. By splitting an event into fragments and recording each from the most appropriate camera position, he coul d importantly vary the stress from camera shot to camera shot. Griffith also achieved impressive effects by means of innovative editing. By juxtaposing images and varying the speed and rhythm of their presentation, he could dominate the impressive intensity of the events as the story developed. Despite the reluctance of his producers, who were afraid that the public would not be able to follow a plot that was made up of such juxtaposed images, Griffith insisted, and experimented as well with other elements of cinematic syntax that have become standard ever since. These contained the flashback, permitting broad psychological and emotive explorati on as well as narrative that was not chronological, and the crosscut between two parallel actions to raise susp ense and excitement. In thus exploiting entirely the possibilities of editing, Griffith transposed devices of the Victorian novel to film and gave film mastery of time as well as space. Besides creating the cinema’s language, Griffith outstandingly expanded its range and treatment of subjects. His initial output was unusually heterogene ous: it included not only the standard comedies, melodramas, westerns, and thrillers, but also such novelties as adaptations from Browning and Tennyson, and treatments of social issues. As his successes climbed, his ambitions grew, and with them the whole of American cinema. When he redesigned Enoch Arden in 1911, he persisted that a subject of such significance could not be treated in the then tranditional length of one reel. Griffith’s introduction of the American-made multireel picture began an enormous revolution. Two years later, Judith of Bethulia, an intricate historicophilosophical spectacle, reached the revolutionary length of four reels, or one hour’s running time. From our current viewpoint, the pretensions of this film may seem a trifle ludicrous, but at the time it stimulated eternal dispute and discussion and gave a fresh intellectual respectability to the cinema.
prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: discuss the importance of Griffith to the development of the cinema
describe the impact on cinema of the flashback and other editing innovations
deplore the state of American cinema before the advent of Griffith
analyze the changes in the cinema wrought by the introduction of the multireel film
document Griffith’s impact on the choice of subject matter in American films

explanation: 正確答案為 A（discuss the importance of Griffith to the development of the cinema）。首句說電影的藝術成熟是 the single-handed accomplishment of David W. Griffith，全文介紹他在構圖、剪輯、題材與多卷片方面的貢獻，即討論他對電影發展的重要性。B、D、E 都只是其中一部分貢獻。

stimulus: Is the literary critic like the poet, responding originality , intuitively, individuality to the written word as the poet responds to human experience? Or is the critic more like a scientist, following a series of demonstrable, confirmable steps, using an unbiased method of analysis? For the woman who is a practitioner of feminist literary criticism, the subjectivity versus impartiality, or critic-as-artist-or-scientist, dispute has unusual importan ce; for her, the question is not merely academic, but political as well, and her definition will court unusual da ngers whichever side of the issue it favors. If she determines feminist criticism as impartial and scientific—a effective, confirmable, intellectual method that anyone, whether man or woman, can perform—the definition not only excludes the critic-as-artist approach, but may also obstruct achievement of the practical political objectives of those who try to alter the academic establishment and its thinking, specially about sex rol es. If she defines feminist criticism as innovative and intuitive, privileged as art, then her work becomes susceptible to the biases of stereotypical opinions about the ways in which women think, and will be dismissed by mu ch of the academic establishment. Because of these biases, women who use an intuitive ap proach in their criticism may find themselves charged with impotence to be analytical, to be impartial, or to think cr itically. Whereas men may be free to claim the role of critic-as-artist, women run various professional dangers when they choose intuition and personal experience as critical method and defense. These questions are political in the sense that the dis pute over them will certainly be less an exploration of conceptual matters in a spirit of unprejudiced inquir y than an academic power struggle in which the careers and professional fortunes of many women scholars—only now joining the academic profession in considerable numbers—will be at stake, and with them the chances for an unique contribution to humanistic understanding, a contribution that might be an significant influence against sexism in our society. As long as the academic establishment continues to re gard disinterested analysis as “masculine” and an intuitive approach as “feminine,” the theoretician must steer a exquisite philosophical course between the two. If she wishes to build a theory of feminist criticism, she would be well advised to place it within the framework of a general theory of the critical process th at is neither purely disinterested nor purely intuitive. Her theory is then more likely to be contrasted and compared with other theo ries of criticism with some degree of unperturbed distance.

A New Theory of Literary Criticism
Literary Criticism: Art or Science?

explanation: 正確答案為 B（Problems Confronting Women Who Are Feminist Literary Critics）。全文聚焦於女性主義批評家無論選擇「科學客觀」或「直覺藝術」的定義，都會「court unusual dangers」，並說明她在學術體制中面臨的專業風險。選項 Literary Criticism: Art or Science? 只是開頭引出的爭論，範圍太廣，未點出女性批評家的特殊困境。

stimulus: A “scientistic” view of language was leading among phi losophers and linguists who affected to produce a scientific analysis of human thought and behavior in the ear ly part of this century. Under the force of this view, it was perhaps unavoidable that the art of rhetoric should pass from the status of being regarded as of controversial worth (because although it might be both a source of delight and a means to motivate people to right action, it might also be a means to distort truth and a source of misguided action) to the status of being wholly censured. If people are regarded only as machines guided by logic, as they were by these “scientistic” thinkers, rhetoric is likely to be held in low regard; for the most evident truth about rhetoric is that it speaks to the whole person. It presents its arguments first to the person as a logical being, because convincing discourse, if fairly conceived, always has a basis in reasoning. Reasonable argument is the plot, as it were, of any speech or essay that is respectfully intended to convince people. Yet it is a characterizing feature of rhetoric that it goes beyond this and attracts the parts of our nature that are involved in feeling, desiring, acting, and suffering. It recollects related instances of the emotive reactions of people to circumstances—real or fictitious—that are similar to our own circumstances. Such is the purpose of both historical accounts and fables in convincing discourse: they suggest literally or symbolically how people may react emotively, with hope or terror, to specific circumstances. A speech at tempting to convince people can obtain little unless it takes into account the aspect of their being relevant to such hopes and terrors. Rhetoric, then, is addressed to human beings living at specific times and in specific places. From the point of view of rhetoric, we are not only rational thinking machines, creatures abstracted from time and space. The study of rhetoric should therefore be considered the most humanistic of the humanities, since rhetoric is not directed merely to our resaonable selves. It takes into account what the “scientistic” view leaves out. If it is a weakness to harbor feelings, then rhetoric may be thought of as dealing in weak point. But those who refuse to the idea of rhetoric becau se they believe it deals in lies and who at the same time hope to move people to action, must either be liars themselves or be very ingenuous; pure logic has never been a stimulating force unless it has been subordinated to human purposes, feelings, and desires, and thereby ceased to be pure logic.

explanation: 正確答案為 B（an indication either of dishonesty or of credulity）。末句說拒斥修辭卻又想推動人們行動的人「must either be liars themselves or be very ingenuous」，即不是不誠實就是天真輕信，正對應 dishonesty or credulity。C 不信任聽眾動機，文中未提。

stimulus: The earliest disagreement about the relationship between photography and art focused on whether photography’s fidelity to appearances and dependence on a machine allowed it to be a fine art as different from only a pragmatic art. Throughout the nineteenth cen tury, the defense of photography was identical with the struggle to form it as a fine art. Against the charge that photography was a soulless, mechanical copying of reality, photographers maintained that it was instead a privileged way of seeing, a revolt against traditional vision, and no less worthy an art than painting. Ironically, now that photography is securely estab lished as a fine art, many photographers find it ostentatious or unrelated to label it as such. Serious phot ographers differently claim to be finding, recording, objectively observing, witnessing events, exploring them selves—anything but making works of art. In the nineteenth century, photography’s combination with th e actual world placed it in an equivocal relation to art; late in the twentieth century, an equivocal relation exis ts because of the Modernist heritage in art. That significant photographers are no longer willing to dispute wh ether photography is or is not a fine art, except to declare that their own work is not involved with art, s hows the extent to which they simply take for granted the notionof art imposed by the triumph of Modernism: the better the art, the more subversive it is of the traditional aims of art. Photographers’ disclaimers of any interest in making art tell us more about the harried status of the contemporary concept of art than about whether photography is or is not art. For instance, those photographers who suppose that, by taking pictures, they are getting away from the pretensions of art as expanded by painting remind us of those Abstract Expressionist pain ters who imagined they were getting away from the intellectual austerity of classical Mode rnist painting by focusing on the physical act of painting. Much of photography’s prestige today derives from the convergence of its aims with those of recent art, especially with the dismissal of abstract art implicit in the pheno menon of Pop painting during the 1960’s. Appreciating photographs is a relief to sensibilities tired of the mental efforts demanded by abstract art. Classical Modernist painting—that is, abstract art as developed in vari ous ways by Picasso, Kandinsky, and Matisse—presupposes greatly developed skills of looking and a familiarity with other paintings and the history of art. Photography, like Pop painting, reassures audiences that art is not difficult; photography seems to be more about its subjects than about art. Photography, however, has developed all the worries and self-consciousness of a classic Modernist art. Many professionals privately have begun to worry that the advancement of photography as an activity subversive of the conventional pretensions of art has gone so far that the public will forget that photography is an unusual and elevated activity—in short, an art.
