stimulus: It is possible for students to attain advanced de grees in English while know ing little or nothing about conventional scholarly measures. The consequences of this neglect of conventional scholarship are especially unfortunate for the study of women writers. If the canon—the list of authors whose works are most widely taught—is ever to contain more women, scholars must be well trained in historical scholarship and textual editing. Scholars who do not know how to read early manuscripts, locate rare books, establish a sequence of editions, and so on are deprived of critical tools for revising the canon. To address such concerns, an experimental version of the conventional scholarly measures course was designated to raise students’ consciousness about the usefulness of conventional learning for any modern critic or theorist. To minimize the artificial aspects of th e traditional course, the usual process of assigning a large number of small problems drawn from the complete range of historical periods was abandoned, though this process has the obvious advantage of at least superfici ally familiarizing students with a comprehensive range of reference sources. Instead students were engaged in a collective effort to do innovative work on a neglected eighteenth-century writer, Elizabeth Griffith, to give th em an authentic experience of literary scholarship and to hearten them to take responsibility for the quality of their own work. Griffith’s work presented a number of advantages for this particular pedagogical intention. First, the body of extant scholarship on Griffith was so diminutive that it could all be read in a day; thereby students spent little time and effort honing the literature and had a clear field for their own discoveries. Griffith’s play The Platonic Wife exists in three versions, enough to furnish illustra tions of editorial issues but not too colossal for beginning students to manage. In ad dition, since Griffith was successful in the eighteenth century, as her continued productivity and favorable reviews esta blish, her exclusion from the canon and virtual disappearance from literary history also helped raise issues concerning the current canon. The range of Griffith’s work meant that each stude nt could become the world’s leading authority on a particular Griffith text. For instance, a student learning Griffith’s Wife in the Right attained a first edition of the play and studied it for some weeks. This student was suitably shocked and out raged to discover its title transformed into A Wife in the Night in Watt’s Bibliotheca Britannica. Such experiences, inevitable and usual in working on a writer to whom so little attention has been paid, serve to vaccinate the student—I hope for a lifetime—against credulous usage of reference sources.

The consequences of this neglect of conventional scholarship are especially unfortunate for the study of women writers. If the canon—the list of authors whose works are most widely taught—is ever to contain more women, scholars must be well trained in historical scholarship and textual editing. Scholars who do not know how to read early manuscripts, locate rare books, establish a sequence of editions, and so on are deprived of critical tools for revising the canon. To address such concerns, an experimental version of the conventional scholarly measures course was designated to raise students’ consciousness about the usefulness of conventional learning for any modern critic or theorist. To minimize the artificial aspects of th e traditional course, the usual process of assigning a large number of small problems drawn from the complete range of historical periods was abandoned, though this process has the obvious advantage of at least superfici ally familiarizing students with a comprehensive range of reference sources. Instead students were engaged in a collective effort to do innovative work on a neglected eighteenth-century writer, Elizabeth Griffith, to give th em an authentic experience of literary scholarship and to hearten them to take responsibility for the quality of their own work. Griffith’s work presented a number of advantages for this particular pedagogical intention. First, the body of extant scholarship on Griffith was so diminutive that it could all be read in a day; thereby students spent little time and effort honing the literature and had a clear field for their own discoveries. Griffith’s play The Platonic Wife exists in three versions, enough to furnish illustra tions of editorial issues but not too colossal for beginning students to manage. In ad dition, since Griffith was successful in the eighteenth century, as her continued productivity and favorable reviews esta blish, her exclusion from the canon and virtual disappearance from literary history also helped raise issues concerning the current canon. The range of Griffith’s work meant that each stude nt could become the world’s leading authority on a particular Griffith text. For instance, a student learning Griffith’s Wife in the Right attained a first edition of the play and studied it for some weeks. This student was suitably shocked and out raged to discover its title transformed into A Wife in the Night in Watt’s Bibliotheca Britannica. Such experiences, inevitable and usual in working on a writer to whom so little attention has been paid, serve to vaccinate the student—I hope for a lifetime—against credulous usage of reference sources.
prompt: Which of the following best states the “partic ular pedagogical purpose” mentioned in line 28?

options.text: To assist scholars in revising the canon of authors
To minimize the trivial aspects of the traditional scholarly methods course
To provide students with information about Griffith’s work
To encourage scholarly rigor in students’ own research
To reestablish Griffith’s reputation as an author

explanation: 正確答案為 D（To encourage scholarly rigor in students’ own research）。前文說課程目的在讓學生獲得真實的學術研究經驗，並「to hearten them to take responsibility for the quality of their own work」，也就是培養研究上的嚴謹。A 是長期目標，C、E 都不是教學目的本身。

stimulus: Proponents of diverse jazz styles have always maintained that their predecessors’ musical style did not include essential features that define jazz as jazz. Therefor e, 1940’s swing was belittled by beboppers of the 1950’s, who were themselves attacked by free jazzers of the 1960’s. The neoboppers of the 1980’s and 1990’s attacked almost everybody else. The titanic figure of Black saxophonist John Coltrane has entangled the arguments made by proponents of styles from bebop through neobop since in his own musical journey he drew from all those styles. His effect on all types of jazz was immeasura ble. At the height of his popularity, Coltrane largely deserted playing bebop, the style that had brought him fame, to exploit the outer reaches of jazz. Coltrane himself probably believed that the merely essential feature of jazz was improvisation, the one steady in his journey from bebop to open-ended improvisations on modal, Indian, and African melodies. On the other hand, this dogged student and prodigious technician—who in sisted on spending hours each day practicing scales from theory books—was never able to jettison entirely the effect of bebop, with its fast and sophisticated chains of notes and ornaments on melody. Two stylistic features shaped the way Coltrane played the tenor saxophone, he pref erred playing fast runs of notes established on a melody and depended on heavy, regularly accented beats. The first led Coltrane to “sheets of sound,” where he raced faster and faster, p ile-driving notes into each other to indicate stacked harmonies. The second meant that his sense of rhythm was almost as close to rock as to bebop. Three recordings exemplify Coltrane’s energizing explorations. Recording Kind of Blue with Miles Davis, Coltrane discovered himself outside bop, exploiting modal melodies. Here he played surging, lengthy solos built largely around repeated motifs—an organizing principle unlike that of free jazz saxophone player Ornette Coleman, who modulated or altered melodies in his solos. On Giant Steps, Coltrane debuted as leader, introducing his own compositions. Here the sheets of sound, downbeat accents, repetitions, and great speed are part of each solo, and the variety of the shapes of his phrases is unique. Coltrane’s searching explorations endangered solid accomplishment. My Favorite Things was another kind of watershed. Here Coltrane played the soprano saxophone, an instrument seldom employed by jazz musicians. Musically, the consequences were astounding. With the soprano’s piping sound, ideas that ha d sounded dark and brooding obtained a feeling of giddy fantasy. When Coltrane started recording for the Impulse! label, he was still searching. His music became raucous, physical. His effect on rockers was immense, including Jimi Hendrix, the rock guitarist, who, following Coltrane, raised the extended guitar solo employing repeated motifs to a style of rock art form.
prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

options.text: discuss the place of Coltrane in the world of jazz and describe his musical explorations
examine the nature of bebop and contrast it with improvisational jazz
analyze the musical sources of Coltrane’s style and their influence on his work
acknowledge the influence of Coltrane’s music on rock music and rock musicians
discuss the arguments that divide the proponents of different jazz styles

explanation: 正確答案為 A（discuss the place of Coltrane in the world of jazz and describe his musical explorations）。文章先說 Coltrane 因 drew from all those styles 而使各派爭論複雜，His effect on all types of jazz was immeasurable，再描述其風格特徵與三張專輯的探索，即討論他在爵士界的地位與音樂探索。C 只對應第三段；D 只是開頭鋪陳。

In effect, scientists already ha ve much of the information required to evaluate the impact of biological control of bracken, but it is spread among many individuals, organizations, and government bodies. Once a biological control agent is released, it is arduous to control its speed. What consideration is due landowners who do not desire to control bracken? stimulus: When we contemplate great painters of the past, the st udy of art and the study of illusion cannot always be separated. By illusion I mean those contrivances of color, line, shape, and so forth that lead us to see marks on a flat surface as depicting three-dimensional objects in space. I must highlight that I am not making a plea, disguised or otherwise, for the exercise of illusionist tricks in painting nowadays , although I am, in effect, rather critical of particular theories of non-representational art. But to argue over these theories would be to miss the point. That the discoveries and effects of represen tation that were the pride of earlier artists have become trivial today I would not deny for a moment. Yet I believe that we are in real danger of losing connection with past masters if we accept the fashionable doctrine that these matte rs never had anything to do with art. The very reason why the representation of nature can now be regarded something commonplace should be of the greatest interest to art historians. Never before has there been an epoch when the visual image was so cheap in every sense of the word. We are surrounded and assaulted by posters and advertisements, comics and magazine illustrations. We see aspects of r eality represented on television, postage stamps, and food packages. Painting is taught in school and practiced as a pastime, and numerous modest amateurs have mastered tricks that would have looked like sheer magi c to the fourteenth-century painter Giotto. Even the crude colored renderings on a cereal box might have ma de Giotto’s contemporaries gasp. Perhaps there are people who conclude from this that the cereal box is supreme to a Giotto; I do not. But I think that the victory and vulgarization of representational skills innovate an issue for both art historians and critics. In this connection it is instructive to recite the Gr eek saying that to marvel is the beginning of knowledge and provided we cease to marvel we may be in danger of ceasing to know. I believe we must restore our sense of wonder at the ability to conjure up by lines, forms, colors, or shades those mysterious phantoms of visual reality we call “pictures.” Even comics and advertisements, correctly viewed, provide food for thought. Just as the study of poetry remains incomplete without an awar eness of the language of prose, so, I believe, the study of art will be increasingly supplemented by inquiry into the “linguistics” of the visual image. The way the language of art refers to the visible world is both so apparent and so mysterious that it is still largely unknown except to artists, who employ it as we employ al l language—without requiring to know its grammar and semantics.

A natural environment that is protected under law because its wildlife has a high economic value

stimulus: The historian Frederick J. Turner wrote in the 1890’s that the agrarian complaint that had been developing steadily in the United States since about 1870 had been ins tigated by the closing of the internal frontier—that is, the depletion of accessible new land needed for furthe r increase of the American farming system. Not only was Turner’s thesis dominant at the time, it was later adopted and elaborated by other scholars, such as John D. Hicks in The Populist Revolt (1931). Actually, however, new lands were used up for farming in the United States throughout and beyond the nineteenth century. In the 1890’s, when agrarian complaint had become most severe, 1,100,000 new farms were settled, wh ich was 500,000 more than had been settled during the antecedent decade. After 1890, under the terms of th e Homestead Act and its successors, more new land was used up for farming than had been used up for this pur pose in the United States up until that time. It is true that a high proportion of the newly farmed land was appropriate only for grazing and dry farming, but agricultural practices had become adequately advanced to make it possible to enhance the profitability of farming by using even these comparatively unproductive lands. The stress given by both scholars and statesmen to the presumed disappearance of the American frontier helped to conceal the great significance of variations in the conditions and conseque nces of international trade that happened during the second half of the nineteenth century. In 1869 the Suez Canal was opened and the first transcontinental railroad in the United States was established. An widespread network of telegraph and telephone communications was spun: Europe was linked by submarine cable with the United States in 1866 and with South America in 1874. By about 1870 devel opment in agricultural technology made possible the entire exploitation of areas that were most suitable for widespread farming on a mechanized basis. Huge tracts of land were being settled and farmed in Argentina, Australia, Canada, a nd in the American West, and these areas were linked with one another and with the countries of Europe into an interdependent market system. As a consequence, agrarian unhappinesses no longer were re gional or national in scope, and they struck many nations whose internal frontiers had not disappered or were not about to disappear. Between the early 1870’s and the 1890’s, the increaseing agrarian complaint in America paralleled the almost continuous decrease in the prices of American agricultural products on foreign ma rkets. Those staple-growing farmers in the United States who demonstrated the greatest complaint were t hose who had become most reliant on foreign markets for the sale of their products. Insofar as Americans ha d been deterred from using up new land for farming, it was because market conditions had made this period a dangerous time in which to do so.

options.text: showing that a certain interpretation is better supported by the evidence than is an alternative explanation
developing an alternative interpretation by us ing sources of evidence that formerly had been unavailable
questioning the accuracy of the evidence that most scholars have used to counter the author’s own interpretation
reviewing the evidence that formerly had been thought to obscure a valid interpretation
presenting evidence in support of a controversial version of an earlier interpretation

explanation: 正確答案為 A（showing that a certain interpretation is better supported by the evidence than is an alternative explanation）。作者先介紹 Turner「邊疆關閉」的論點，接著以 Actually, however 用新土地持續開墾的數據反駁，再主張國際貿易與市場價格才是農民不滿的真因。B 的「先前無法取得的證據」文中未提。

Actually, however, new lands were used up for farming in the United States throughout and beyond the nineteenth century. In the 1890’s, when agrarian complaint had become most severe, 1,100,000 new farms were settled, wh ich was 500,000 more than had been settled during the antecedent decade. After 1890, under the terms of th e Homestead Act and its successors, more new land was used up for farming than had been used up for this pur pose in the United States up until that time. It is true that a high proportion of the newly farmed land was appropriate only for grazing and dry farming, but agricultural practices had become adequately advanced to make it possible to enhance the profitability of farming by using even these comparatively unproductive lands. The stress given by both scholars and statesmen to the presumed disappearance of the American frontier helped to conceal the great significance of variations in the conditions and conseque nces of international trade that happened during the second half of the nineteenth century. In 1869 the Suez Canal was opened and the first transcontinental railroad in the United States was established. An widespread network of telegraph and telephone communications was spun: Europe was linked by submarine cable with the United States in 1866 and with South America in 1874. By about 1870 devel opment in agricultural technology made possible the entire exploitation of areas that were most suitable for widespread farming on a mechanized basis. Huge tracts of land were being settled and farmed in Argentina, Australia, Canada, a nd in the American West, and these areas were linked with one another and with the countries of Europe into an interdependent market system. As a consequence, agrarian unhappinesses no longer were re gional or national in scope, and they struck many nations whose internal frontiers had not disappered or were not about to disappear. Between the early 1870’s and the 1890’s, the increaseing agrarian complaint in America paralleled the almost continuous decrease in the prices of American agricultural products on foreign ma rkets. Those staple-growing farmers in the United States who demonstrated the greatest complaint were t hose who had become most reliant on foreign markets for the sale of their products. stimulus: In the early 1950’s, historians who investigaed preindustr ial Europe (which we may define here as Europe in the period from roughly 1300 to 1800) began, for the first time in large numbers, to study more of the preindustrial European population than the 2 or 3 per cent who comprised the political and social elite: the kings, generals, judges, nobles, bishops, and regional magnates who had hitherto frequently filled history books. One difficulty, however, was that few of the rema ining 97 percent recorded their thoughts or had them chronicled by contemporaries. Faced with this situa tion, many historians based their examinations on the merely records that seemed to exist: birth, marriage, and death records. As a result, much of the early work on the nonelite was aridly statistical in nature; decreasing the extensive majority of the population to a set of numbers was hardly more illuminating than neglecting th em altogether. Historians still did not know what these people thought or felt. One way out of this dilemma was to turn to the records of legal courts, for here the voices of the nonelite can most often be heard, as witnesses, plaintiffs, an d defendants. These documents have acted as “a point of entry into the mental world of the poor.” Historians such as Le Roy Ladurie have utilized the documents to extract case histories, which have lightened the attitud es of distinct social groups (these attitudes include, but are not limited to, attitudes toward crime and the law) and have disclosed how the authorities administered justice. It has been societies that have had a developed police system and practiced Roman law, with its written depositions, whose court records have yielded the most data to historians. In Anglo-Saxon countries hardly any of these advantages obtain, but it has still b een possible to glean information from the study of legal documents. The extraction of case histories is not, however, the merely use to which court records may be put. Historians who study preindustrial Europe have used the records to form a series of categories of crime and to quantify indictments that were issued over a given number of years. This use of the records does yield some information about the nonelite, but this information giv es us little insight into the psychological lives of the nonelite. We also realize that the number of indictment s in preindustrial Europe bears little relation to the number of real criminal acts, and we greatly dount th at the relationship has changed broadly over time. In addition, aggregate population estimates are greatly unst eady, which makes it difficult for historians to contrast rates of crime per thousand in one decade of the preindustrial period with rates in another decade. Given these deficiencies, it is understandable why the case history use of court records is to be preferred.

Used investigatory methods that were almost exclusively statistical in nature.
Inaccurately estimated the influence of the preindustrial European political and social elite.
Confined their work to a narrow range of the preindustrial European population.
Tended to rely heavily on birth, marriage, and death records.

explanation: 正確答案為 D（Confined their work to a narrow range of the preindustrial European population.）。文中說 1950 年代初史家 began, for the first time in large numbers 研究菁英以外的人口，而過去的史書多半只寫占 2 至 3% 的國王、將軍、貴族等，可見先前研究範圍狹窄。B、E 的統計與出生死亡紀錄是 1950 年代後研究非菁英時才採用的方法。

stimulus: The first mention of slavery in the statutes of the Eng lish colonies of North America does not occur until after 1660—some forty years after the import of the first Black people. Lest we think that slavery existed indeed before it did in law, Oscar and Mary Handlin ensure us that the status of Black people down to the 1660’s was that of servants. A crticism of the Handlins’ explanati on of why legal slavery did not appear until the 1660’s indicates that presumptions about the relation between sl avery and racial bias should be reviewd, and that interpretations for the various treatment of Black slaves in North and South America should be extended. The Handlins interpret the appearance of legal slavery by arguing that, during the 1660’s, the position of White servants was promoting related to that of Black servants. Thus, the Handlins maintain, Black and White servants, heretofore treated alike, each attained a distinct status. There are, however, significant rejections to this argument. First, the Handlins cannot sufficiently illustrate that the White servant’s position was enhancing during and after the 1660’s; several acts of the Maryland a nd Virginia legislatures suggest otherwise. Another flaw in the Handlins’ explanation is their presumptions that prior to the establishment of legal slavery there was no prejudice against Black people. It is true that before the 1660’s Black people were hardly called slaves. But this should not obscure evidence from the 1630’s on that points to racial discrimination without using the term slavery. Such prejudice sometimes ped short of lifetime servitude or inherited status—the two attributes of true slavery—yet in other cases it included both. The Handlins’ ar gument precludes the actual possibility that Black people in the English colonies were never treated as the equals of White people. This possibility has significant ramifications. If from the outset Black people were discriminated against, then legal slavery should be treated as a reflection and an extension of racial discrimination rather than, as many historians including the Handlins have contended, the cause of discrimination. In addition, the existence of prejudice before the advent of legal slavery provid es a further interpretation for the bitter treatment of Black slaves in North than in South America. Freyre and Tannenbaum have correctly contended that the lack of certain conventions in North America—such as a Ro man notion of slavery and a Roman Catholic stress on equality—interprets why the treatment of Black slaves was more serious there than in the Spanish and Portuguese colonies of South America. But this cannot be the whole interpretation since it is only passive, based only on a lack of something. A more convincing interpretation is that the early and sometimes exceeding racial prejudice in the English colonies helped determine the special nature of the slavery that followed.

stimulus: A long-held view of the history of the English colonies that became the United States has been that England’s policy toward these colonies before 1763 was dictated by business benefits and that a change to a more sovereign policy, controlled by expansionist militarist objectives, produced the tensions that finally caused the American Revolution. In a recent study, Stephen Saunde rs Webb has held a strong opposition to this idea. According to Webb, England already had a military imperial policy for more than a century before the American Revolution. He sees Charles II, the Eng lish monarch between 1660 and 1685, as the correct successor of the Tudor monarchs of the sixteenth century and of Oliver Cromwell, all of whom were bent on expanding centralized executive power over England’s possessions through the use of what Webb calls “garrison government.” Garrison government allowed the co lonists a judicial assembly, but real authority, in Webb’s view, belonged to the colonial governor, who was appointed by the king and buttressed by the “garrison,” that is, by the regional contingent of English troops under the colonial governor’s command. According to Webb, the purpose of garrison government was to offer military support for a royal policy designed to restrict the power of the upper classes in th e American colonies. Webb contends that the colonial legislative assemblies stood for the interests not of th e ordinary people but of the colonial upper classes, a coalition of merchants and nobility who supported self-rule and sought to promote legislative authority at the expense of the executive. It was, according to Webb, the colonial governors who supported the small farmer, resisted the plantation system, and tried through taxati on to break up huge holdings of land. Backed by the military presence of the garrison, these governors tried to k eep the gentry and merchants, allied in the colonial assemblies, from transforming colonial America into a capitalistic oligarchy. Webb’s study illustrates the political alignments that occurred in the colonies in the century prior to the American Revolution, but his view of the crown’s use of the military as an instrument of colonial policy is not totally persuasive. England during the seventeenth century was not not ed for its military accomplishments. Cromwell did mount England’s most aspiring overseas military expedition in more than a century, but it proved to be an utter debacle. Under Charles II, the English army was too small to be a vital instrument of government. Not until the war with France in 1697 did William III convince Parliament to create a professional standing army, and Parliaments price for doing so was to keep the army under tight legislative control. While it may be correct that the crown attempted to reduce the power of the colonial upper classes, it is hard to conceive how the English army during the seventeenth century coul d have offered important military support for such a policy.

stimulus: Discussion of the assimilationof Puerto Ricans in the United States has conc entrated on two factors: social standing and the loss of national culture. In general, excessi ve pressure is placed on one factor or the other, relying on whether the commentator is North Ameri can or Puerto Rican. Many North American social scientists, such as Oscar Handlin, Joseph Fitzpatrick, an d Oscar Lewis, consider Puerto Ricans as the most recent in a long line of ethnic entrants to occu py the lowest rung on the social ladder. Such a “sociodemographic” approach tendencies to regard assimilation as a benign process, taking for granted enhanced economic advantage and unavoidable cultural integration, in a supposedly egalitarian context. However, this approach fails to take into account the co lonial nature of the Puerto Rican case, with this group, unlike their European precursors, coming from a nation politically subjected to the United States. Even the “radical” critiques of this mainstream research model, such as the critique developed in Divided Society , attach the issue of ethnic assimilation too mechanically to factors of economic and social mobility and are thus unable to lighten the cultural subordination of Puerto Ricans as a colonial minority. In contrast, the “colonialist” approach of island-based writers such as Eduardo Seda-Bonilla, Manuel Maldonado-Denis, and Luis Nieves-Falcon tends to consider assimilation as the forced loss of national culture in an unequal contest with imposed foreign values. There is, of course, a strong convention of cultural accommodation among other Puerto Rican thinkers. The writings of Eugenio Fernandez Mendez certainly promoted this tradition, and many advocates of Pu erto Rico’s commonwealth status share the same universalizing orientation. But the Puerto Rican inte llectuals who have written most about the assimilation process in the United States all advance cultural nati onalist views, supporting the preservation of minority cultural distinctions and opposing what they see as the conquest of colonial nationalities. This cultural and political emphasis is suitable, but th e colonialist thinkers misdirect it, ignoring the class relations at work in both Puerto Rican and North Ameri can history. They pose the clash of national cultures as an complete polarity, with each culture comprehended as invariable and undifferentiated. Yet both the Puerto Rican and North American conventions have been subject to continuous challenge from cultural forces within their own societies, forces that may move toward each other in ways that cannot be written off as mere “assimilation.” Consider, forinstance, the indigenous and Afro-Caribbean conventions in Puerto Rican culture and how they influence and are influenced by other Ca ribbean cultures and Black cultures in the United States. The components of coercion and inequality, so vital to cu ltural contact according to the colonialist framework play no role in this kind of convergence of racially and ethnically various elements of the same social class.

support the thesis that assimilation has not been a benign process for Puerto Ricans

indicate deficiencies in two schools of though t on the assimilation of Puerto Ricans in the United States
reject the attempt to formulate a general frame work for discussion of the assimilation of Puerto Ricans in the United States

explanation: 正確答案為 D（indicate deficiencies in two schools of…）。作者先批評北美 sociodemographic approach fails to take into account the colonial nature，再說 colonialist 學者的強調 suitable 但 misdirect it, ignoring the class relations，即指出兩派的不足。C 誘人，但作者明確批評文化民族主義觀點把文化視為 invariable；A 只涵蓋前半。

stimulus: Simone de Beauvoir’s work immensely influenced Betty Friedan’s—Indeed, made it true. Why, then, was it Friedan who became the prophet of women’s emancipa tion in the United States? Political conditions, and a certain anti-intellectual bias, prepared Americans and the American media to better accept Friedan’s deradicalized and highly pragmatic The Feminine Mystique, released in 1963, than Beauvoir’s theoretical reading of women’s situation in The Second Sex. In 1953 when The Second Sex first appeared in translation in the United States, the country had entered the silent, fearful fortress of the anticommunist McCarthy years (1950-1954), and Beauvoir was suspicious of Marxist sympathies. Even The Nation , a typically liberal magazine, warned its readers against “certain political leanings” of the author. Open acknowledgement of the existence of women’s oppression was too radical for the United States in the fifties, and Beauvoir’s conclusion, that change in women’s economic condition, though inad equate by itself, “remains the basic factor” in developing women’s situation, was especially unacceptable.

concentrates on the practical aspects of the questions of women’s emancipation

explanation: 正確答案為 E（concentrates on the practical aspects of the questions of women’s emancipation）。作者說美國人較能接受 Friedan「deradicalized and highly pragmatic」的書，而非 Beauvoir「theoretical reading」，差別在於前者著重實際面向。B 把兩本書的特徵對調了；A 則缺乏根據。

stimulus: Astoundingly enough, modern historians have rarely interested themselve s in the history of the American South in the epoch before the South began to beco me self-consciously and distinctively “Southern”—the decades after 1815. As a result, the cultural history of Br itain’s North American empire in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries has been written almost as if the Southern colonies had never existed. The American culture that emerged during the Colonial and Revolutionary periods has been depicted as having been simply an extension of New England Puritan culture. Howeve r, Professor Davis has recently asserted that the South stood apart from the rest of American society during this early era, following its own unique pattern of cultural growth. The case for Southern distinctiveness rests upon two connected premises: first, that the cultural similarities among the five Southern colonies were far more impressive than the discrepancies, and second, that what made those colonies alike also made them disparate from the other colonies. The first, for which Davis offers an immense amount of evidence, can be accepted without major reservations; the second is far more problematic. What makes the second premise problematic is th e usage of the Puritan colonies as a basis for comparison. Quite properly, Davis decries the exceeding influence ascribed by historians to the Puritans in the formation of American culture. Yet Davis inadvertently adds weight to these ascriptions by employing the Puritans as the standard against which to assess the acco mplishments and contributions of Southern colonials. Throughout, Davis focuses on the significant, and undeniable, discrepancies between the Southern and Puritan colonies in motives for and patterns of early settlement, in attitudes toward nature and Native Americans, and in the degree of receptivity to metropolitan cultural influences. However, recent scholarship has highly suggested th at those aspects of early New England culture that seem to have been most distinctly Puritan, such as the strong religious orientation and the communal impulse, were not even typical of New England in general, but were largely confined to the two colonies of Massachusetts and Connecticut. Therefore, what in cont rast to the Puritan colonies appears to Davis to be peculiarly Southern—acquisitiveness, a st rong interest in politics and the law, and a tendency to generate metropolitan cultural models—was not only more generally English than the cultural patterns displayed by Puritan Massachusetts and Connecticut, but also almost certainly characteristic of most other early modern British colonies from Barbados north to Rhode Island a nd New Hampshire. Within the larger framework of American colonial life, then, not the Southern but the Puritan colonies appear to ha ve been distinctive, and even they seem to have been rapidly assimilating to the dominant cultural patterns by the late Colonial epoch.

challenging the hypothesis that early American culture was homogeneous in nature
challenging the contention that the American Sout h made greater contributions to early American culture than Puritan New England did

explanation: 正確答案為 B（refuting a thesis about the distinctiveness of the culture of the early American South）。作者接受 Davis 的第一前提，卻質疑第二前提，結論是「not the Southern but the Puritan colonies」才獨特，即反駁南方獨特論。選項「反駁兩個前提」錯，作者明言第一前提可以接受。

stimulus: Students of United States history, seeking to identify the circumstances that heartened the emergence of feminist movements, have completely investigated th e mid-nineteenth-century American economic and social conditions that affected the status of women. These historians, however, have analyzed less thoroughly the development of specifically feminist ideas and activities during the same period. Furthermore, the ideological origins of feminism in the United States have been obscu red since, even when historians did take into account those feminist concepts and activities occurring within th e United States, they failed to realize that feminism was then a truly international movement actually centere d in Europe. American feminist activists who have been portrayed as “solitary” and “individual theorists” were in reality related to a movement—utopian socialism—which was already popularizing feminist concepts in Europe du ring the two decades that culminated in the first women’s rights conference he ld at Seneca Falls, New York, in 1848. Therefore, a complete understanding of the origins and development of nineteenth-century feminism in the United States requires that the geographical focus be widened to contain Europe and that the detailed study already made of social conditions be expanded to contain the ideological growth of feminism. The earliest and most popular of the utopian socia lists were the Saint-Simonians. The specifically feminist part of Saint-Simonianism has, however, been less researched than the group’s contribution to early socialism. This is regrettable on two counts. By 1832 feminism was the central concern of Saint-Simonianism and completely absorbed its adherents’ energy; thus, by ignoring its feminism, European historians have misunderstood Saint-Simonianism. Furthermore, b ecause many feminist concepts can be traced to Saint-Simonianism, European historians’ appreciation of later feminism in France and the United States remained restricted. Saint-Simon’s followers, plenty of whom were women, based their feminism on an interpretation of his project to reorganize the globe by replacing brute force w ith the rule of spiritual powers. The new world order would be ruled together by a male, to represent re flection, and a female, to represent sentiment. This complementarity reflects the fact that, while the Saint-Si monians did not deny the belief that there were innate discrepancies between men and women, they neverthel ess foresaw an equally significant social and political role for both sexes in their utopia. Merely a few Saint-Simonians opposed a definition of sexual equality based on gender distinction. This minority believed that individuals of both sexes were born similar in ability and character, and they ascribed male-female discrepancies to socialization and educa tion. The envisioned consequence of both currents of thought, however, was that women would enter public life in the new era and that sexual equality would reward men as well as women with an ameliorated way of life.

explanation: 正確答案為 A（insufficiently familiar with the international origins of…）。作者說這些史家「failed to realize that feminism was then a truly international movement actually centered in Europe」，而被稱為「solitary」的美國女權者其實與歐洲 utopian socialism 有關聯。C 方向相反：作者主張應擴大而非縮小地理範圍。

stimulus: It is frequently assumed that the mechanization of work has a revolutionary infl uence on the lives of the people who operate the new machines and on the society into which the machines ha ve been introduced. For instance, it has been suggested that the employment of women in industry took them out of the household, their conventional sphere, and fundamentally altered their position in society. In the nineteenth century, when women started to enter factories, Jules Simon, a Fr ench politician, warned that by doing so, women would jettison their femininity. Friedrich Engels, however, predicted that women would be liberated from the “social, legal, and economic subordina tion” of the family by technological developments that made possible the recruitment of “the whole female sex into public indu stry.” Observers thereby differed concerning the social desirability of mechanization’s influences, but they admitted that it would transform women’s lives. Historians, especially those investigating the history of women, now seriously question this assumption of transforming power. They conclude that such dram atic technological creations as the spinning jenny, the sewing machine, the typewriter, and the vacuum cleaner have not led to equally dr amatic social changes in women’s economic position or in the prevailing estim ation of women’s work. The employment of young women in textile mills during the Industrial Revolution was largely an extension of an older pattern of employment of young, single women as domestics. It w as not the change in office technology, but rather the separation of secretarial work, previously seen as an apprenticeship for beginning managers, from administrative work that in the 1880’s created a new class of “dead-end” jobs, thenceforth regarded “women’s work.” The accretion in the numbers of married women employed outside the home in the twentieth century had less to do with the mechanization of housework an d an accretion in leisure time for these women than it did with their own economic necessity and with high marriage rates that shrank the available pool of single women workers, previously, in numerous cases, the only women employers would hire. Women’s work has altered considerably in the past 200 years, moving from the household to the office or the factory, and later becoming mostly white-collar instead of blue-collar work. Basically, however, the conditions under which women work have altered little since before the Industrial Revolution: the segregation of occupations by gender, lower pay for women as a group, jobs that demand relatively low levels of skill and offer women little change for advanc ement all persist, while women’s household labor remains challenging. Recent historical investigation has led to a main revisi on of the notion that technology is always inherently revolutionary in its effects on society. Mechanization may even have slowed any change in the conventional position of women both in the labor market and in the home.
prompt: Which of the following statements best summarizes the main idea of the passage?

options.text: The effects of the mechanization of women’ s work have not borne out the frequently held assumption that new technology is inherently revolutionary.

Mechanization has caused the nature of women’s work to change since the Industrial Revolution.
The mechanization of work creates whole new classes of jobs that did not previously exist.
The mechanization of women’s work, while extrem ely revolutionary it its effects, has not, on the whole, had the deleterious effects that some critics had feared.

explanation: 正確答案為 A（The effects of the mechanization of women’ s work have not borne out the frequently held assumption that new technology is inherently revolutionary.）。作者引述史家研究，說明紡紗機、打字機等發明並未帶來同等劇烈的社會變化，結論是修正「科技必然具革命性」的觀念。C 只說工作性質改變，未觸及主旨。

stimulus: In an ideally free and open market economy, the type of employer—government or private—should have little or no impact on the earnings differentials between wo men and men. However, if there is discrimination against one sex, it is unlikely that the degree of discr imination by government and private employers will be the same. Discrepancies in the degree of discrimination would lead to earnings differentials associated with the type of employer. Given the nature of governme nt and private employers, it seems most likely that discrimination by private employers would be greater. Th erefore, one would expect that, if women are being discriminated against, government employment w ould have a positive influence on women’s earnings as compared with their earnings from private employment. The consequences of a study by Fuchs support this assumption. Fuchs’s results suggest that the earnings of women in an industry composed completely of government employers would be 14. 6 percent greater th an the earnings of women in an industry composed exclusively of private employees, other things being equal. In addition, both Fuchs and Sanborn have suggested that the influence of discrimination by consumers on the earnings of self-employed women may be larger th an the influence of either government or private employer discrimination on the earnings of women employees. To test this theory, Brown selected a large sample of White male and female workers from the 197 0 Census and separated them into three categories: private employees, government employees, and self-emp loyed. (Black workers were excluded from the sample to prevent picking up earnings differentials that were the consequence of racial disparities.) Brown’s research design controlled for education, labor-force partic ipation, motivation, mobility, and age in an attempt to eliminate these factors as explications of the study ’s results. Brown’s results suggest that men and women are not treated the same by employers and consumers. For men, self-employment is the highest earnings category, with private employment next, and government lowest. For women, this order is reversed. One can infer from Brown’s consequences that consumers discriminate against self-employed women. Moreover, self-employed women may have more difficulty than men in receiving good employees and may encounter discrimination from suppliers as well as from financial institutions. Brown’s results are clearly correspondent with Fuch’s argument that discrimination by consumers has a larger impact on the earnings of women than does discrimination by either government or private employers. stimulus: One of the fundamental themes of Walzer’s criticism of liberal capitalism is that it is insufficient egalitarian. Walzer’s case against the economic inequality developed by capitalism and support “a radical redistribution of wealth” is presented in a widely cited essay entitled “In Defense of Equality.” The most noticeable characteristic of Walzer’s criticis m is that, far from fighting against the principle of reward according to merit, Walzer persists on its valid ity. People who excel should obtain the superior merits appropriate to their preeminence. But people exhibit a great diversity of qualities—“intelligence, physical strength, agility and grace, artistic inventiveness, mechanical skill, leader ship, endurance, memory, psychological discernment, the capacity for arduous wo rk—even moral strength, sensitivity, the ability to convey sympathy.” Each deserves its proper recompense, and hence a proper distribution of material goods should demonstrate human distinctions as measured on all these various scales. Yet, under capitalism, the ability to make money (“the green thumb of bourgeois society”) makes its possessor obtain nearly “every other sort of social good,” such as the esteem and respect of others. The centerpiece of Walzer’s argument is the invocation of a citation from Pascal’s Pensees, which concludes: “Tyranny is the wish to acquire by one mean s what can merely be had by another.” Pascal believes that we owe various duties to various qualities. So we might say that infatuation is the proper response to charm, and awe the proper response to strength. In this light, Walzer distinguishes capitalism as the tyranny of money (or of the ability to make it). And Walzer s upports as the means of removing this tyranny and of restoring real equality “the abolition of the power of money outside its sphere.” Wh at Walzer envisions is a society in which wealth is no longer exchangeable into social goods with which it has no inherent association. Walzer’s argument is a astonishing one. After a ll, why should those qualities unassociated with the production of material goods be rewarded with material goods? Is it not dictatorial, in Pascal’s sense, to persist that those who excel in “sensitivity” or “the ability to convey sympathy” merit equal wealth with those who excel in qualities (such as “the capacity for hard work”) essential in producing wealth? Yet Walzer’s argument, however insufficient, does point to one of the most severe weaknesses of capitalism—namely, that it brings to dominant positions in a society people who, no matter how legitimately they have obtained their material rewards, often lack those other qualities that evoke tributes or veneration. Some ev en contend believably that this weakness may be unmanageable: in any society that, like a capitalist societ y, seeks to become ever wealthier in material terms disproportionate rewards ar e bound to flow to the people who are instrumental in creating the increment in its wealth.

stimulus: One of the fundamental themes of Walzer’s criticism of liberal capitalism is that it is insufficient egalitarian. Walzer’s case against the economic inequality developed by capitalism and support “a radical redistribution of wealth” is presented in a widely cited essay entitled “In Defense of Equality.” The most noticeable characteristic of Walzer’s criticis m is that, far from fighting against the principle of reward according to merit, Walzer persists on its valid ity. People who excel should obtain the superior merits appropriate to their preeminence. But people exhibit a great diversity of qualities—“intelligence, physical strength, agility and grace, artistic inventiveness, mechanical skill, leader ship, endurance, memory, psychological discernment, the capacity for arduous wo rk—even moral strength, sensitivity, the ability to convey sympathy.” Each deserves its proper recompense, and hence a proper distribution of material goods should demonstrate human distinctions as measured on all these various scales. Yet, under capitalism, the ability to make money (“the green thumb of bourgeois society”) makes its possessor obtain nearly “every other sort of social good,” such as the esteem and respect of others. The centerpiece of Walzer’s argument is the invocation of a citation from Pascal’s Pensees, which concludes: “Tyranny is the wish to acquire by one mean s what can merely be had by another.” Pascal believes that we owe various duties to various qualities. So we might say that infatuation is the proper response to charm, and awe the proper response to strength. In this light, Walzer distinguishes capitalism as the tyranny of money (or of the ability to make it). And Walzer s upports as the means of removing this tyranny and of restoring real equality “the abolition of the power of money outside its sphere.” Wh at Walzer envisions is a society in which wealth is no longer exchangeable into social goods with which it has no inherent association. Walzer’s argument is a astonishing one. After a ll, why should those qualities unassociated with the production of material goods be rewarded with material goods? Is it not dictatorial, in Pascal’s sense, to persist that those who excel in “sensitivity” or “the ability to convey sympathy” merit equal wealth with those who excel in qualities (such as “the capacity for hard work”) essential in producing wealth? Yet Walzer’s argument, however insufficient, does point to one of the most severe weaknesses of capitalism—namely, that it brings to dominant positions in a society people who, no matter how legitimately they have obtained their material rewards, often lack those other qualities that evoke tributes or veneration. Some ev en contend believably that this weakness may be unmanageable: in any society that, like a capitalist societ y, seeks to become ever wealthier in material terms disproportionate rewards ar e bound to flow to the people who are instrumental in creating the increment in its wealth.

stimulus: Human relations have commanded people’s attention from early times. The ways of people have been recorded in incalculable myths, folktales, novels, po ems, plays, and popular or philosophical essays. Although the full importance of a human relationship may not be directly obvious, the complication of feelings and actions that can be comprehended at a glance is as tonishingly great. For this reason psychology holds a distinctive position among the sciences. “Intuitive” knowledge may be noticeably penetrating and can importantly help us comprehend hum an behavior, whereas in the phy sical sciences such commonsense knowledge is comparatively primitive. If we erased all knowledge of scientific physics from our modem word, not only would we not have cars and television sets, we might even discover that the common person was unable to address the essential mechanical problems of pulleys and levers. On the other hand if we eliminated all knowledge of scientific psychology from our world, pr oblems in interpersonal relations might simply be addressed and solved much as before. We would still “know” how to avoid doing something asked of us and how to get someone to agree with us; we would still “know” when someone was angry and when someone was delighted. One could even provide sensible interpreta tions for the “whys” of much of the self’s behavior and feelings. In other words, the common person has a great and deep comprehension of the self and of other people which, though unformulated or only approximately imagined, enables one to interface with others in more or less adaptive ways. Kohler, in referring to the lack of great discoveries in psychology as compared with physics, explains this by saying that “people were acquainted with actually all territories of mental life a long time before the founding of scientific psychology.” Paradoxically, with all this natural, intuitional, commonsense capacity to seize human relations, the science of human relations has been one of the last to develop. Various interpretati ons of this contradiction have been indicated. One is that science would dama ge the vain and pleasant illusions people have about themselves; but we might ask why people have alwa ys loved to read depressed, debunking writings, from Ecclesiastes to Freud. It has also been argued that just because we know so much about people intuitively, there has been less inducement for st udying them scientifically; why should one develop a theory, carry out methodical observations, or make projections about th e obvious? In any case, the field of human relations, with its extensive literary documentation but scanty scientific treatment, is in great contradiction to the field of physic in which there are comparatively few nonscientific books.
prompt: According to the passage, it has been suggested that the science of hum an relations was slow to develop because

options.text: intuitive knowledge of human relations is derived from philosophy
early scientists were more interested in the physical world
scientific studies of human relations appear to investigate the obvious
the scientific method is difficult to apply to the study of human relations
people generally seem to be more attracted to literary than to scientific writings about human relations

explanation: 正確答案為 C（scientific studies of human relations appear to investigate the obvious）。文末提到一種解釋：正因我們直覺上懂得很多，就少有研究動機，「why should one…make projections about the obvious?」。選項「人們較愛讀文學而非科學作品」不是文中提出的原因，作者提到人們愛讀悲觀揭露性作品，是用來反駁「保護幻想」的說法。

stimulus: Defenders of unusual preservative labor legislation for women often contend that eliminating such laws would damage the fruits of a century-long struggle for the pr otection of women workers. Even a concise scrutiny of the historic practice of courts and employers would show that the fruit of such laws has been bitter: they are, in practice, more of a curse than a blessing. Sex-defined protective laws have often been b ased on conventional presumptions concerning women’s needs and abilities, and employers have usually used th em as legal excuses for discriminating against women. After the Second World War, for instance, businesses and government tried to convince women to vacate jobs in factories, thus making room in the labor force for returning veterans. The revival or passage of state laws restricting the daily or weekly work hours of wome n conveniently accomplished this. Employers had just to declare that overtime hours were an important condition of employment or promotion in their factory, and women could be quite legally fired, rejected to jobs, or kept at low wage levels, all in the name of “protecting” their health. By validating such laws when they are qu estioned by lawsuits, the c ourts have colluded over the years in establishing various, less advantageous employ ment terms for women than for men, thus decreasing women’s competitiveness on the job market. At the same time, even the most well-intentioned lawmakers, courts, and employers have often been blind to the real needs of women. The lawmakers and the courts continue to allow employers to provide employee health insurance plans that cover all known human medical disabilities except those relating to pregnancy and childbirth. Eventually, labor laws protecting just unusual groups are often inefficient at protecting the workers who are actually in the workplace. Some chemicals, for instance, pose reproductive hazards for women of childbearing years; manufacturers using the chemicals comply with laws preserving women against these risks by rejecting to hire them. Thus the sex-defined legi slation defends the hypothetical female worker, but has no impact whatever on the safety of any real employee. Th e health risks to male employees in such industries cannot be insignificant, since chemicals poisonous enough to cause birth defects in fetuses or sterility in women are possibly detrimental to the human metabo lism. Protective laws aimed at altering production materials or techniques in order to decline such h azards would benefit all employees without discriminating against any. In sum, protective labor laws for women are prejudicial and do not meet their intended purpose. Legislators should discover that women are in the work force to stay, and that their needs—good health care, a satisfactory wage, and a secure workplace—are the needs of all workers. Laws that neglect these facts violate women’s rights for equal protection in employment.

The health of most women factory workers improved.
Employment practices that addressed the real needs of women workers became common.

The history may be too confident because most of its data date from the 1880’s at the la test, and the information provided from that decade is inadequately analyzed. Conditions in fact reduced in the 1880’s, and continued to decrease after the 1880’s, due to a reorganization of the packing process and a mass ive influx of untrained workers. The degeneration in worker status, partly a result of the new accessibilit y of untrained and hence low-priced labor, is not considered. Though a comprehensive account of work in th e packing-houses is attempted, the author fails to differentiate between the wages and conditions for prof icient workers and for those untrained laborers who comprised the majority of the industry’s workers from the 1880’s on. While conditions for the former were probably tolerable due to the strategic significant of proficient workers in the intricate slaughtering, cutting, and packing process (though worker complaints about the ra te and conditions of work were frequent), pay and conditions for the latter were wretched. The writer’s misunderstanding of the origins of the feelings the meat-packers had for their industrial neighborhood may explain the history’s faulty generali zations. The pride and contentment the writer remarks upon were, probably, less the products of the industrial world of the packers—the giant yards and the complex plants—than of the unity and vibrance of the ethni c cultures that established a feasible community on Chicago’s South Side. Indeed, the strength of this community succeeded in developing a social movement that efficaciously confronted the problems of the industry that provided its livelihood.

stimulus: Although Victor Turner’s writings have proved prolific for fields beyond anthropology, his definition of ritual is excessively restrained. Ritual, he says, is “prescr ibed formal behavior for occasions not given over to technological routine, having reference to beliefs in mysterious beings or powers.” “Technological routine” refers to the means by which a social group provides for its material needs. Turner’s differentiating ritual from technology helps us acknowledge that f estivals and celebrations may have little purpose other than play, but it conceals the pragmatic aims, such as making crops grow or healing patients, of other rituals. Further, Turner’s definition indicates an important relationship between ritual and mystical beliefs. However, not all rituals are religious; some religions have no re ference to mystical beings; and individuals may be required merely to participate in, not importantly believe in, a ritual. Turner ’s supposition that ritual behavior follows belief thus restricts the usefulness of his definition in studying ritual across cultures.

stimulus: The evolution of sex ratios has endangered, in most plants and animals with separate sexes, approximately equal numbers of males and females. Why should this be so? Two major kinds of answers have been offered. One is couched with respect to advant age to population. It is asserted that the sex ratio will evolve so as to maximize the number of meetings between individua ls of the opposite sex. This is essentially a “group selection” argument. The other, and in my view right, type of answer was first put forward by Fisher in 1930. This “genetic” argument begins from the assumption that genes can affect the relative numbers of male and female offspring produced by an individual carrying the genes. That sex ratio will be favored which maximizes the number of descendants an individual will ha ve and thus the number of gene copies transmitted. Suppose that the population consisted mostly of females: then an individual who produced sons merely would have more grandchildren. On the contrary, if the population consisted mostly of mal es, it would pay to have daughters. If, however, the population consisted of equal numbers of males and females, sons and daughters would be evenly valuable. Thus a one-to-one sex ratio is the only constant ratio; it is an “evolutionarily stable strategy.” Even though Fisher wrote before the mathema tical theory of games had been developed, his theory incorporates the essential characteristic of a game—that th e best strategy to adopt lies in what others are doing. Since Fisher’s time, it has been recognized that genes can sometimes affect the chromosome or gamete in which they discover themselves so that the gamete will be more likely to participate in fertilization. If such a gene appears on a sex-determining (X or Y) chromosome, then highly aberrant sex ratios can appear. But more immediately relevant to game theory are the sex ratios in specific parasitic wasp species that have a large excess of females. In these species, fertilized eggs grow into females and unfertilized eggs into males. A female stores sperm and can decide the sex of each egg she lays by fertilizing it or leaving it unfertilized. By Fisher’s argument, it should still pay a female to produ ce equal numbers of sons and daughters. Hamilton, noticing that the eggs develop within their host—th e larva of another insect—and that the newly emerged adult wasps mate immediately and disperse, proposed a remarkably cogent analysis. Because only one female often lays eggs in a given larva, it would pay her to produce one male only, since this one male could fertilize all his sisters on emergence. Like Fisher, Hamilton sought for an evolutionarily stable strategy, but he went a step further in recognizing that he was seeking for a strategy.

stimulus: The evolution of intelligence amid early large mammals of the grasslands was due in great measure to the interaction between two ecologically synchronized groups of these animals, the hunting carnivores and the herbivores that they hunted. The interaction arising from the differences between predator and prey led to a general improvement in brain functions; however, speci fic components of intelligence were ameliorated far more than others. The kind of intelligence favored by the interplay of increasingly smarter catchers and increasingly keener escapers is defined by attention—that aspect of mind carrying consciousness forward from one moment to the next. It varies from an inactive, free-floating awareness to a highly focused, energetic fixation. The range through these states is mediated by the arousal system, a network of tracts converging from sensory systems to integrating centers in the brain stem. From the more sluggish to the more vigorous levels, sensitivity to novelty is increased. The organism is more awake, more vigilant; this increased vigilance accounts for the apprehension of ever more subtle signals as the organism becomes more sensitive to its surroundings. The procedure of arousal and concentration give attention its direction. Arousal is at first general, with a flooding of impulses in the brain stem; then gradually the activati on is channeled. Therefore begins concentration, the holding of consistent images. One meaning of intelligence is the way in which such images and other alertly searched information are employed in the context of previous experience. Consciousness connects past attention to the present and allows the integration of details with perceived ends and intentions. The elements of intelligence and consciousness come together marvelously to generate disparate styles in predator and prey. Herbivores and carnivores develop different kinds of attention correlated to escaping or chasing. Even though in both kinds of animal, ar ousal stimulates the production of adrenaline and norepinephrine by the adrenal glands, the effect in herbivores is primarily dread, whereas in carnivores the effect is primarily aggression. For both, arousal attunes the animal to what is ahead. Perhaps it does not experience forethought as we know it, but the animal does experience something like it. The predator is searchingly aggressive, innerdirected, tuned by the nervous system and the adrenal hormones, but aware in a sense closer to human consciousness than, say, a hungr y lizard’s instinctive snap at a passing beetle. Harnessing past events as a framework, the large ma mmal predator is working out a relationship between movement and food, sensitive to possibilities in cold trails and remote sounds—and yesterday’s unforgotten lessons. The herbivore prey is of a disparate mind. Its mood of wariness instead of searching and its attitude of general expectancy rather than anticipating are silk -thin veils of tranquility ove r an explosive endocrine system.

stimulus: Numerous theories have been formulated to explicate th e role of grazers such as zooplankton in governing the amount of planktonic algae (phytoplankton) in lakes. The first theories of such grazer control were only based on observations of negative correlations between algal a nd zooplankton numbers. A low number of algal cells in the presence of a high number of grazers indicated, bu t did not substantiate, that the grazers had removed most of the algae. The converse observation, of th e absence of grazers in areas of high phytoplankton concentration, led Hardy to proffer his principle of an imal exclusion, which hypothesized that phytoplankton generated a repellent that excluded grazers from regions of high phytoplankton concentration. This was the first suggestion of algal defenses against grazing. Perhaps the fact that plenty of these first studies consid ered merely algae of a size that could be collected in a net (net phytoplankton), a practice that overlooke d the smaller phytoplankton (nannoplankton) that we now know grazers are most likely to feed on, accounted for a de-emphasis of the role of grazers in subsequent research. Increasingly, as in the individual studies of Lund, Round, and Reynolds, researchers started to emphasize the significance of environmental factors such as light, temperature, and water movements in controlling algal numbers. Th ese environmental factors were amenable to field monitoring and to simulation in the laboratory. Grazing was believed to have so me influences on algal numbers, particularly after phytoplankton growth rates decreased at the end of bloom periods, but grazing was regarded a minor component of models that predicted algal population dynamics. The potential magnitude of grazing pressure on freshwater phytoplankton has merely recently been determined empirically. Studies by Hargrave and Geen assessed natural community grazing rates by measuring feeding rates of individual zooplankton species in the laboratory and then computing community grazing rates for field conditions utilizing the known pop ulation density of grazers. The high evaluations of grazing pressure postulated by these researchers were not completely accepted, however, until the grazing rates of zooplankton were determined directly in the field, by means of novel experimental techniques. Harnessing a specially prepared feeding chamber, Hane y was able to record zooplankton grazing rates in natural field conditions. In the periods of peak zooplankton abundance, that is, in the late spring and in the summer, Haney recorded maximum daily community gr azing rates, for nutrient-poor lakes and bog lakes, respectively, of 6.6 percent and 114 percent of daily phytoplankton production. Cladocerans had higher grazing rates than copepods, often leading to 80 pe rcent of the community grazing rate. These rates ranged seasonally, reaching the lowest point in the winter a nd early spring. Haney’s thorough research provides cogent field evidence that grazers can exert important pressure on phytoplankton population.

stimulus: Two comparatively recent independent developments stand behind the current major research effort on nitrogen fixation, the procedure by which bacteria sy mbiotically render leguminous plants independent of nitrogen fertilizer. The one development has been the rapid, sustained increase in the price of nitrogen fertilizer. The other development has been the rapid grow th of knowledge of and technical sophistication in genetic engineering. Fertilizer prices, largely tied to the price of natural gas, huge amounts of which go into the manufacture of fertilizer, will continue to represent an immense and escalating economic burden on modern agriculture, stimulating the search for alternativ es to synthetic fertilizers. And genetic engineering is only the sort of fundamental breakthrough that opens up prospects of entirely novel alternatives. One such innovative idea is that of inserting into the chromosomes of plants discrete genes that are not a part of the plants’ natural constitution: particularly, the idea of inser ting into nonleguminous plants the genes, if they can be identified and isolated, that fit the leguminous plants to be hosts for nitrogen-fixing bacteria. Therefore, the intensified research on legumes. Nitrogen fixation is a procedure in which certain b acteria utilize atmospheric nitrogen gas, which green plants cannot directly use, to produce ammonia, a nitr ogen compound plants can utilize. It is one of nature’s great ironies that the availability of nitrogen in the so il frequently sets an upper limit on plant growth even if the plants’ leaves are bathed in a sea of nitrogen gas. The leguminous plants—amidst them crop plants such as soybeans, peas, alfalfa, and clover—have resolved the nitrogen supply problem by entering into a symbiotic relationship with the bacterial genus Rhizobium ; in effect, there is a specific strain of Rhizobium for each species of legume. The host plant provides the bacteria with food and a protected habitat and receives surplus ammonia in exchange. Thereby, legumes can thrive in nitrogen-depleted soil. Unfortunately, most of the major food crops—including rice, wheat, maize, and potatoes—cannot. In contrast, plenty of the high-yielding hybrid varieties of these food crops bred during the Green Revolution of the 1960’s were chosen specifically to give high yields in response to generous applications of nitrogen fertilizer. This poses an additional, formidable challenge to plant geneticists: they must work on enhancing fixation within the existing symbioses. Unless they succeed, the yield gain s of the Green Revolution will be intensely lost even though the genes in legumes that equip those plants to en ter into a symbiosis with nitrogen fixers are identified and isolated, and even though th e transfer of those gene complexes, once they are discovered, becomes possible. The overall task looks fo rbidding, but the stakes are too high not to undertake it.

explain the reasons for and the objectives of current research on nitrogen-fixing symbioses
describe the nature of the genes that regulate the symbiosis between legumes and certain bacteria

explanation: 正確答案為 D（explain the reasons for and the objectives of current research on nitrogen-fixing symbioses）。首段說兩項發展（肥料價格上漲、基因工程進步）stand behind 目前的固氮研究，之後說明研究目標：把共生能力轉移到非豆科作物並強化現有共生。全文在解釋研究的原因與目的。B、C 只是文中細節或作者並未論證的主張；A 的「脆弱基礎」過於偏離。

stimulus: Recent findings indicate that visual signals are fed into at least three different processing systems in the brain, each with its own clear function. One system appears to process information about form perception; a second, information about color; a third, information about movement, location, and spatial organization. An comprehension of the functions and capabilities of th ese three systems can shed light on how artists manipulate materials to create astonishing visual effects. It is possible to sum up the functions of the three su bsystems of the visual system as follows. The parvo system carries greatly comprehensive information about static objects and about borders that are shaped by contrasting colors. It does not, however, carry inform ation about particular colors. Because much of the information about the shape of objects can be portrayed by their borders, we observe that this system is significant in shape perception. The blob system proce sses information about colors, but not about movement, form discrimination, or depth. The magno system carries information about movement and depth. It is good at observing motion but poor at examining static images. In addition it appears to be colorblind; it is unable to discern borders that are visible only on the basis of color contrast. Cells in the parvo system can discern between two colo rs at any relative brightness of the two. Cells in the color-blind magno system, on the other hand, are si milar to a black-and-white photograph in the way they function: they signal information about the brightness of surfaces but not about their colors. For any pair of colors there is a special brightness ratio at which tw o colors, for instance red and green, will appear as the similar shade of gray in a black-and-white photograph, hence any border between them will vanish. Similarly at some relative red-to-green brightness level, the red and green will appear unanimous to the magno system. The red and green are then called equiluminant. A border between two equiluminant colors has color contrast but no luminance contrast. Many artists have seemed to be empirically aware of these fendamental principles and have used them to maximize special effects. Some of the special effect s of Op Art, for instance, probably arise from color combinations that are strong activators of the parvo sy stem but are weak stimulant for the magno system. An object that is equiluminant with its background look s dynamic and unsteady. The reason is that the parvo system can signal the object’s shape but the magno system cannot see its borders and therefore cannot signal either the movement or the position of the object. Hence it seems to jump around, drift, or vibrate on the canvas.

options.text: describing subsystems of the visual system and showing their relevance to art
comparing three theories on how the visual system analyzes images in a work of art
explaining how artists use color contrasts to create particular visual effects
explaining how the visual system distinguishes among different colors
describing functions of the first three phases of the visual system

explanation: 正確答案為 A（describing subsystems of the visual system and showing their relevance to art）。文章先說明 parvo、blob、magno 三系統的功能，再解釋 Op Art 等藝術效果的原理。C 只涵蓋最後一段的應用；E 錯在三者是平行系統，而非依序的「phases」。
